nodes.name: Algebraic integer iff minimal polynomial integral
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in K$ be an algebraic number with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$. Then $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer if and only if $m_{\alpha}$ has integer coefficients (note that it will be monic by the definition of minimal polynomial).
assumptions: $\alpha \in K$ be an algebraic number with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$
conclusions: $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer if and only if $m_{\alpha}$ has integer coefficients

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer, then its an algebraic number, so I claim that $m_\alpha$ is monic with integer coefficient. We know $\alpha$ satisfies some some monic polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients and therefore $m_\alpha$ divides $f(x)$. Now use the monic Gauss lemma \ref{monic gauss} to get that $m_\alpha$ is in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Conversely, if $m_\alpha$ is has integer coefficients, then $\alpha$ satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, thus is an algebriac integer.

nodes.name: Integers in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be a square free integer and let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ then \[\mathcal{O}_K= \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{d}] & \text{ if } d\equiv 2 \text{ or } 3 \pmod 4 \\ \mathbb{Z}[\frac{1+\sqrt{d}}{2}] & \text{ if } d\equiv 1 \pmod 4 \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)}$ is $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt d]$ for $d\equiv 2,3$ and $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt d)/2]$ for $d\equiv 1 \bmod 4$.
assumptions: Let $d$ be a square free integer and let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$
nodes.label: thm: int quad field

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha=a+b\sqrt{d}$ with $a,b \in \mathbb{Q}$. If $b=0$ then we are just asking which rational numbers are algebraic integers, which we have seen are only the integers. So assume $b \neq 0$. Then the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is \[x^2-2ax+ (a^2-db^2).\] Therefore, $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer if and only if $2a$ and $(a^2-db^2)$ are integers. Now, since $2a$ is an integer, we have $4a^2$ is an integer, and thus $d(2b)^2$ must be an integer. If $2b$ was not an integer, then a $p^2$ (for some prime $p$) would appear in the denominator of $(2b)^2$. This would force $d$ to be divisible by $p^2$ contradicting the square-free assumption. Thus $2b \in \mathbb{Z}$. So let $u=2a,v=2b$. Then we have $u^2-dv^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. Now, if $v$ is even, then so is $u$ in which case $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$. So assume $v$ is odd, we need to show this can only happen if $d \equiv 1 \mod 4$. Now, $v^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and $u^2$ is either $0,1 \pmod 4$. But note it can't be zero since $d$ cant be $0 \pmod 4$ as its square-free, therefore $u^2 \equiv 1 \mod 4$ and hence $d \equiv 1 \mod 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrality iff $2a$ and $a^2-db^2$ are integers; square-freeness forces $2b\in\mathbb{Z}$, then a parity analysis mod 4.

nodes.name: Finitely generated as an abelian group
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$. We say $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is finitely generated as an abelian group if there exits a finite set $\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ of elements $b_i \in \mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ such that every element of $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ may be written in the form \[x_1b_1+\cdots+x_nb_n\] with $x_i \in \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Algebraic integers via finitely generated groups
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item[(1)] $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer. \item[(2)] As an additive group, $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is finitely generated. \item[(3)] $\alpha$ is an element of some subring of $\mathbb{C}$ having a finitely generated additive group. \item[(4)] $\alpha A \subset A$ with $A \subset \mathbb{C}$ some finitely generated additive subgroup. Here $\alpha A$ is the set of elements of the form $\alpha x$ for $x \in A$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: TFAE: $\alpha$ integral; $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ finitely generated; $\alpha$ in a f.g. subring; $\alpha A\subset A$ for some f.g. subgroup $A$.
equivalent_conditions: As an additive group, $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is finitely generated.
$\alpha$ is an element of some subring of $\mathbb{C}$ having a finitely generated additive group.
$\alpha A \subset A$ with $A \subset \mathbb{C}$ some finitely generated additive subgroup.
assumptions: $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$
nodes.label: thm: alg ints fin gen

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: $(1) \implies (2)$ : Since $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer, it is the root of the monic polynomial $m_\alpha$ of degree $n$, say, which has integer coefficients. In this case we claim that $\{1,\alpha,\cdots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ is generates $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$. For this we note that if $f(\alpha) \in \mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$, then by doing polynomial long division we have $f(x)=q(x)m_\alpha(x)+r(x)$ with $\deg(r)<n$. Now if evaluate at $\alpha$ we get $f(\alpha)=r(\alpha)$. But since $\deg(r)<n$ we see that $r(\alpha)$ is in the $\mathbb{Z}$ span of $\{1,\alpha,\cdots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$. Thus giving the claim. $(2)\implies (3) \implies (4)$ : This is trivial. It remains to prove $(4) \implies (1)$. Let $\{a_1,\dots,a_r\}$ be a basis of $A$. Then as each $\alpha a_i \in A$ we can again write it in terms of this basis, so we get a system of equations \begin{align*} \alpha a_1 &=x_{1,1} a_1+\cdots+x_{1,r}a_r \\ \alpha a_2 &=x_{2,1} a_1+\cdots+x_{2,r}a_r \\ &\vdots \\ \alpha a_r &=x_{r,1} a_1+\cdots+x_{r,r}a_r \\ \end{align*} with the $x_{i,j} \in \mathbb{Z}$. If we write this in matrix form by setting $X={x_{i,j}}$, $a=(a_1,\dots,a_r)$ then we have \[X a^{T}=\alpha a^{T}\] (here $()^T$ denotes transpose). Therefore, $\alpha$ is an eigenvalue of $X$, which is a matrix with integer entries. Thus by Lemma \ref{lem: roots of int matrix alg ints} we must have that $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer.
nodes.statement_short: (1)$\Rightarrow$(2) by long division by $m_\alpha$; (4)$\Rightarrow$(1) since $\alpha$ is an eigenvalue of an integer matrix.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha,\beta$ are algebraic integers, then by Theorem \ref{thm: alg ints fin gen} $(2)$ we have $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ and $\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ are finitely generated (as additive groups). Moreover, the ring $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha,\beta]$ (take this to be defined as the smallest ring containing $\mathbb{Z},\alpha,\beta$) is also finitely generated, since if $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ generate $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ and $\{b_1,\dots,b_m\}$ generates $\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ then $\{a_ib_j\}_{i,j}$ generates $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha,\beta]$. Now, $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha,\beta]$ contains both $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha\beta$, then \ref{thm: alg ints fin gen} $(3)$ tells us that they must also be algebraic integers.

nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be an extension of number fields and assume that $\alpha \in K$ is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_F$. Prove that $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer.
nodes.label: quest: ints in tower law

nodes.name: Norm and trace of algebraic integers are integers
nodes.statement: If $K$ is a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ and $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ are both in $\mathbb{Z}$.
assumptions: If $K$ is a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$
nodes.label: prop: norm trace of alg int is int

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{cor: field pol of alg int has int coefs} we know $C_\alpha$ has integer coefficients and therefore by Proposition \ref{prop: field pol relation to norm and trace} we get the result.
nodes.statement_short: $C_\alpha$ has integer coefficients, which are $\pm$ trace and norm.

nodes.name: A_alpha need not be integral
nodes.statement: Note that if $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer then $A_\alpha$ need not have integer entries. It possible that in different bases the matrix $A_\alpha$ does not have integer entries. What is true is that in any basis the norm and trace will always be integers as the corollary shows.

nodes.name: Integer norm and trace do not imply integrality
nodes.statement: The converse is not true. For example $\frac{\sqrt{1+\sqrt{17}}}{2}$ has integer norm and trace, but it is not an algebraic integer.

nodes.name: Z[alpha] is contained in O_K
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$, then $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha] \subset \mathcal{O}_K$.
assumptions: Let $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$,

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer and by definition it is contained in $K$, we have $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$, from which the result follows by Definition \ref{definition: Z alpha}.

nodes.name: O_K need not be monogenic
nodes.statement: If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ is a number field, then is it not always the case that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ as we can see from Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field}. You might ask if its possible to always find some algebraic integer $\alpha'$ such that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha']$ but this is also not true. There are rings of integers that are not generated by a single element. For example, if $\alpha$ is a root of $x^3+x^2-2x-8$, then one can show that if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ then $\mathcal{O}_K$ is never of the form $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha']$ for any algebraic integer $\alpha'$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{O}_K$ need not equal $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$, nor be monogenic at all (root of $x^3+x^2-2x-8$).

nodes.name: UFD subrings generating K equal O_K
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $R$ be a subring of $\mathcal{O}_K$ which generates $K$ as a field (i.e. $Frac(R)=K$). If $R$ has unique factorization, then $R=\mathcal{O}_K$.
nodes.statement_short: A UFD subring of $\mathcal{O}_K$ with fraction field $K$ is all of $\mathcal{O}_K$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let $R$ be a subring of $\mathcal{O}_K$ which generates $K$ as a field (i.e. $Frac(R)=K$).

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We know that $R \subset \mathcal{O}_K$, we will show the opposite inclusion. Let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Then since $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ we can find $\delta,\gamma \in R$ such that $\alpha=\frac{\gamma}{\delta}$, with $\delta,\gamma$ sharing no common factors other than a unit. Now, since $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer, we can find some monic polynomial such that \[\alpha^n+a_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0.\] If we now multiply through by $\delta^n$ we get \[\gamma^n+a_{n-1}\gamma^{n-1}\delta+\cdots+a_0\delta^n=0.\] Since $R$ is assumed to have unique factorization, we see that if $\varpi$ is an irreducible factor of $\delta$, then $\varpi$ is an irreducible factor of $\gamma^n$ and thus is a factor of $\gamma$. But we assumed that $\delta,\gamma$ shared no common factors other than units. So $\delta$ has no irreducible factors and is therefore a unit. So $\mathcal{O}_K \subset R$, giving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\alpha=\gamma/\delta$ in lowest terms; the integral equation forces every irreducible factor of $\delta$ to divide $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Remains: $\mathcal{O}_K\subset R$
nodes.statement: We know that $R \subset \mathcal{O}_K$, we will show the opposite inclusion.

nodes.name: Write $\alpha=\gamma/\delta$ coprime
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Then since $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ we can find $\delta,\gamma \in R$ such that $\alpha=\frac{\gamma}{\delta}$, with $\delta,\gamma$ sharing no common factors other than a unit.

nodes.statement_short: Clear denominators in the integral equation

nodes.name: Irreducible factors of $\delta$ divide $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Since $R$ is assumed to have unique factorization, we see that if $\varpi$ is an irreducible factor of $\delta$, then $\varpi$ is an irreducible factor of $\gamma^n$ and thus is a factor of $\gamma$.

nodes.name: $\delta$ is a unit
nodes.statement: But we assumed that $\delta,\gamma$ shared no common factors other than units. So $\delta$ has no irreducible factors and is therefore a unit. So $\mathcal{O}_K \subset R$, giving the result.

nodes.name: Integral basis
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a basis for $K/\mathbb{Q}$. We call this an integral basis if $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[b_1,\dots,b_n]=\{x_1b_1+\cdots x_nb_n \mid x_i \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ as an additive group. In practice, the set $\{b_i\}$ will be some thing like $\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ in which case, as rings, we have $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]=\mathbb{Z}[1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}]$
nodes.label: definition: int basis

nodes.name: Discriminant of a set of elements
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a set of elements in $K$. The discriminant of $B$ is defined as \[\Delta(B)= \det \left (\begin{matrix} \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_1b_1) &\cdots& \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_1b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_nb_1) &\cdots& \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_nb_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\] If needed we will denote the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_1b_1) &\cdots& \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_1b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_nb_1) &\cdots& \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_nb_n) \end{matrix} \right )\] by $T_B$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of {1, sqrt d}
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d$ square-free. Then lets take $B=\{1,\sqrt{d}\}$ which is our basis for $K$. Then we have \[\Delta(B)=\det \matrd{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(1)}{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{d})}{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{d})}{\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(d)} =\det \matrd{2}{0}{0}{2d}=4d\]

nodes.name: Nonzero discriminant iff linearly independent
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a set of elements in $K$. Then $\Delta(B) \neq 0$ if and only if the elements in $B$ are linearly independent.
equivalent_conditions: the elements in $B$ are linearly independent
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and let $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a set of elements in $K$
conclusions: $\Delta(B) \neq 0$ if and only if the elements in $B$ are linearly independent

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First recall from linear algebra, that if we have a finite dimensional vector space $V$ with a non-degenerate bilinear form $\langle, \rangle$ on $V$, then $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ a basis of $V$ if and only if \[\det \left (\begin{matrix} \langle v_1, v_1 \rangle &\cdots& \langle v_1,v_n \rangle \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \langle v_n,v_1\rangle &\cdots& \langle v_n,v_n\rangle \end{matrix} \right ) \neq 0.\] (This matrix appearing here is called the matrix associated to the pairing $\langle,\rangle$ with respect to our chosen basis). Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: tr perfect} we know that the trace pairing is perfect, which in particular means it is non-degenerate. Moreover, $\Delta(B)$ is exactly the determinant of the matrix associated to the trace pairing. So, we see that $B$ consists on linearly independent vectors if and only if $\Delta(B) \neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The Gram determinant of a non-degenerate form detects bases; the trace form is perfect.

nodes.name: Gram determinant criterion for bases
nodes.statement: First recall from linear algebra, that if we have a finite dimensional vector space $V$ with a non-degenerate bilinear form $\langle, \rangle$ on $V$, then $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ a basis of $V$ if and only if \[\det \left (\begin{matrix} \langle v_1, v_1 \rangle &\cdots& \langle v_1,v_n \rangle \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \langle v_n,v_1\rangle &\cdots& \langle v_n,v_n\rangle \end{matrix} \right ) \neq 0.\] (This matrix appearing here is called the matrix associated to the pairing $\langle,\rangle$ with respect to our chosen basis).

nodes.name: Trace pairing is non-degenerate
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: tr perfect} we know that the trace pairing is perfect, which in particular means it is non-degenerate.

nodes.statement: Moreover, $\Delta(B)$ is exactly the determinant of the matrix associated to the trace pairing. So, we see that $B$ consists on linearly independent vectors if and only if $\Delta(B) \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Discriminant change of basis
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B,B'$ bases for $K/\mathbb{Q}$. If $P$ denotes the change of basis matrix, then \[\Delta(B)=\det(P)^2 \Delta(B').\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $B,B'$ bases for $K/\mathbb{Q}$.
nodes.label: prop: disc change of basis

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $T_B=(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_i b_j))_{i,j}$ be the matrix associated to the trace pairing with respect to $B$. Then, it is a basic result in linear algebra that if you have the matrix associated to a bilinear pairing and change the basis, then the matrix gets conjugated by the change of basis matrix. This means that $T_B=P^{t}T_{B'}P$, (where $()^t$ denotes transpose). Now, taking determinants we get $\Delta(B)=\det(T_B)=\det(P^t T_{B'}P)=\det(P^t)\det(T_{B'})\det(P)$ which gives the result once you remember that $\det(P^t)=\det(P)$.

nodes.name: Change of basis conjugates the Gram matrix of the trace pairing
nodes.statement: Let $T_B=(\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_i b_j))_{i,j}$ be the matrix associated to the trace pairing with respect to $B$. Then, it is a basic result in linear algebra that if you have the matrix associated to a bilinear pairing and change the basis, then the matrix gets conjugated by the change of basis matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Change of basis conjugates the Gram matrix of the trace pairing

nodes.name: Take determinants
