nodes.name: Discriminant of algebraic integers is an integer
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be elements in $\mathcal{O}_K$, then $\Delta(B) \in \mathbb{Z}$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be elements in $\mathcal{O}_K$,
nodes.label: prop: int basis int disc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $b_i b_k$ is an algebraic integer, then $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_i b_j) \in \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore the matrix $T_B$ has integers coefficients, and therefore the determinant is a integer.
nodes.statement_short: Traces of algebraic integers are integers, so $T_B$ is integral.

nodes.name: Integral elements need not give an integral basis
nodes.statement: Just because we take a basis consisting of algebraic integers, it doesn't mean that it is an integral basis. To find an integral basis we need to be a bit more careful.

nodes.name: Discriminant test for integral bases
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a basis for $K/\mathbb{Q}$ consisting of algebraic integers. If $B$ is not an integral basis then there exists an algebraic integer of the form \[\alpha=\frac{x_1b_1+\cdots+x_nb_n}{p}\] where $p$ is a prime and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ with not all $x_i$ zero. Moreover, if $x_i \neq 0$ and we let $B'$ be the basis obtained by replacing $b_i$ with $\alpha$, then \[\Delta(B')= \frac{x_i^2}{p^2} \Delta(B).\] In particular $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$.
nodes.statement_short: If an algebraic-integer basis is not integral, some $(\sum x_ib_i)/p$ is integral; swapping it in divides $\Delta$ by $p^2/x_i^2$, so $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$.
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a basis for $K/\mathbb{Q}$ consisting of algebraic integers
If $B$ is not an integral basis
if $x_i \neq 0$ and we let $B'$ be the basis obtained by replacing $b_i$ with $\alpha$
conclusions: there exists an algebraic integer of the form
nodes.label: lem: disc int basis

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $B$ is not an integral basis then we can find some element $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with not all the $y_i$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. So, let $N$ be the least common multiple of the denominators of the $y_i$ (meaning $Ny_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$). Now, let $p$ be a prime factor of $N$. If we now consider $(N/p)\phi$ then all of the coefficients of $b_i$ are in $\frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$ (so they have denominator $1$ or $p$.) and at least one of them has denominator $p$ (since not all the $y_i$ where in $\mathbb{Z}$). So by relabelling, wlog we can assume \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with $y_i \in \frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$ Now look at \[\psi:=\lfloor y_1 \rfloor b_1+\cdots+\lfloor y_n \rfloor b_n\] (here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of $x$). The both $\psi$ and $\phi$ are algebraic integers (as the $b_i$ are algebraic integers). Therefore, so is $\theta=\phi-\psi$. By construction, $\theta$ has coefficients of the for $\frac{x_i}{p}:=y_i-\lfloor y_i \rfloor$ where $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and not all the $x_i$ are zero (since, again, not all the $y_i$ were in $\mathbb{Z}$). This gives the first part of the lemma. Now, assume $x_i \neq 0$, then let us replace $b_i \in B$ with $\theta$ to get a new basis $B'$ which again consists of algebraic integers. Next, we note that the change of basis matrix from $B$ to $B'$ is \[ \left( \begin{matrix} 1&0&\cdots& \frac{x_1}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ 0&1&\cdots& \frac{x_2}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ \vdots& \vdots&&\vdots&&\vdots \\ 0&0&\cdots& \frac{x_n}{p}& \cdots &1 \\ \end{matrix} \right) \](here the column of $x_j/p$'s is in the $i$-th column). This matrix has determinant $\frac{x_i}{p}.$ Therefore, by Proposition \ref{prop: disc change of basis} we see that $\Delta(B')=\frac{x_i^2}{p^2}\Delta(B)$. But both $\Delta(B),\Delta(B')$ are in $\mathbb{Z}$ by Proposition \ref{prop: int basis int disc}, therefore $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ giving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce a non-integral element to coefficients in $\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$, subtract integer parts, then compute the change-of-basis determinant $x_i/p$.

nodes.name: Take an integral element with non-integer coordinates
nodes.statement: If $B$ is not an integral basis then we can find some element $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with not all the $y_i$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take an integral element with non-integer coordinates

nodes.name: Let $N$ be the common denominator
nodes.statement: So, let $N$ be the least common multiple of the denominators of the $y_i$ (meaning $Ny_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$).

nodes.name: Scale by $N/p$: denominators $1$ or $p$
nodes.statement: Now, let $p$ be a prime factor of $N$. If we now consider $(N/p)\phi$ then all of the coefficients of $b_i$ are in $\frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$ (so they have denominator $1$ or $p$.) and at least one of them has denominator $p$ (since not all the $y_i$ where in $\mathbb{Z}$).

nodes.name: WLOG coefficients in $\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: So by relabelling, wlog we can assume \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with $y_i \in \frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Subtract integer parts $\psi$
nodes.statement: Now look at \[\psi:=\lfloor y_1 \rfloor b_1+\cdots+\lfloor y_n \rfloor b_n\] (here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of $x$).

nodes.name: $\theta=\phi-\psi$ is integral
nodes.statement: The both $\psi$ and $\phi$ are algebraic integers (as the $b_i$ are algebraic integers). Therefore, so is $\theta=\phi-\psi$.

nodes.name: First part of the lemma
nodes.statement: By construction, $\theta$ has coefficients of the for $\frac{x_i}{p}:=y_i-\lfloor y_i \rfloor$ where $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and not all the $x_i$ are zero (since, again, not all the $y_i$ were in $\mathbb{Z}$). This gives the first part of the lemma.

nodes.name: Replace $b_i$ by $\theta$
nodes.statement: Now, assume $x_i \neq 0$, then let us replace $b_i \in B$ with $\theta$ to get a new basis $B'$ which again consists of algebraic integers.

nodes.name: Change-of-basis matrix
nodes.statement: Next, we note that the change of basis matrix from $B$ to $B'$ is \[ \left( \begin{matrix} 1&0&\cdots& \frac{x_1}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ 0&1&\cdots& \frac{x_2}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ \vdots& \vdots&&\vdots&&\vdots \\ 0&0&\cdots& \frac{x_n}{p}& \cdots &1 \\ \end{matrix} \right) \](here the column of $x_j/p$'s is in the $i$-th column).

nodes.name: Discriminant scales by $x_i^2/p^2$
nodes.statement: This matrix has determinant $\frac{x_i}{p}.$ Therefore, by Proposition \ref{prop: disc change of basis} we see that $\Delta(B')=\frac{x_i^2}{p^2}\Delta(B)$.

nodes.name: Integrality of discriminants gives $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$
nodes.statement: But both $\Delta(B),\Delta(B')$ are in $\mathbb{Z}$ by Proposition \ref{prop: int basis int disc}, therefore $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ giving the result.

nodes.name: Existence of an integral basis
nodes.statement: There exists a (finite) integral basis in $K$.
nodes.label: cor: int basis exists

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: The fact that it is finite follows from $K$ being a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$. Let $B$ be a basis consisting of algebraic integers, now by repeatedly applying Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis}, we can obtain $B$ such that $\mid \Delta(B) \mid $ is as small as possible. This must now be an integral basis, otherwise Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} would allow us to find a new basis $B'$ with $|\Delta(B')| < |\Delta(B)|$ contradicting our choice of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $|\Delta(B)|$ over algebraic-integer bases; the lemma would otherwise decrease it.

nodes.name: Finiteness from $[K:\mathbb{Q}]<\infty$
nodes.statement: The fact that it is finite follows from $K$ being a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

nodes.name: Take a basis minimizing $|\Delta(B)|$
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a basis consisting of algebraic integers, now by repeatedly applying Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis}, we can obtain $B$ such that $\mid \Delta(B) \mid $ is as small as possible.

nodes.name: Minimality contradicts the lemma otherwise
nodes.statement: This must now be an integral basis, otherwise Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} would allow us to find a new basis $B'$ with $|\Delta(B')| < |\Delta(B)|$ contradicting our choice of $B$.

nodes.name: Square-free discriminant implies integral basis
nodes.statement: If $B$ is a basis consisting of integral elements and $\Delta(B)$ is square-free, then $B$ is an integral basis.
assumptions: If $B$ is a basis consisting of integral elements and $\Delta(B)$ is square-free,
nodes.label: cor: square free implies int basis

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This follows at once from Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis}.

nodes.name: Converse fails: Z[i]
nodes.statement: Note that the converse is not true! For example if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-1})$ then $B=\{1,\sqrt{-1}\}$ is an integral basis, but $\Delta(B)=-4$ which is not square-free.

nodes.name: Algorithm for finding an integral basis
nodes.statement: Note that this also gives us an algorithm for finding an integral basis as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Pick $B$ a basis consisting of algebraic integers and calculate $\Delta(B)$. \item For each prime $p$ such that $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ we can use Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} to get a new basis $B'$ with smaller discriminant. \item Now, repeat step one. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively improve an algebraic-integer basis at primes $p$ with $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$ using the discriminant lemma.

nodes.name: Pick an algebraic-integer basis and compute $\Delta(B)$
nodes.statement: Pick $B$ a basis consisting of algebraic integers and calculate $\Delta(B)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick an algebraic-integer basis and compute $\Delta(B)$

nodes.name: Use the lemma at each $p$ with $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$
nodes.statement: For each prime $p$ such that $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ we can use Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} to get a new basis $B'$ with smaller discriminant.
nodes.statement_short: Use the lemma at each $p$ with $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Now, repeat step one.

nodes.name: Integral basis of Q(sqrt5)
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ and take $B=\{1,\sqrt{5}\}$. Then we have $\Delta(B)=2^2\cdot5$. So, if we apply Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} we get a new basis $B'=\{1,\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\}$ which has discriminant $5$, which is square-free, and therefore is a basis of $\mathcal{O}_K$.

nodes.name: Integral bases have equal discriminants
nodes.statement: Let $B,B'$ be two integral bases of a number field $K$. Then $\Delta(B)= \Delta(B')$.
assumptions: Let $B,B'$ be two integral bases of a number field $K$.
nodes.label: prop: int bases disc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: In this case the change of basis matrix from $B$ to $B'$ is an invertible matrix with integer coefficients, so its determinant is $\pm 1$. Using Proposition \ref{prop: disc change of basis}, we see that a change of basis matrix won't alter the discriminant, since the factor of the determinant squared is what appears.
nodes.statement_short: Change of basis matrix is in $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$, determinant $\pm1$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a number field
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field, and let $B$ be an integral basis. Then we define the discriminant of $K$ as $\Delta(B)$. Note that by Proposition \ref{prop: int bases disc}, this definition does not depend on the choice of integral basis. So we will sometimes denote it simply by $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)$.
nodes.label: definition: disc of num field

nodes.name: Discriminant via embeddings
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Now let $M$ be the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \sigma_1(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_1(b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \sigma_n(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_n(b_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\] Then \[\Delta(B)=\det(M)^2.\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Now let $M$ be the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \sigma_1(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_1(b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \sigma_n(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_n(b_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\]
nodes.label: prop: disc via embs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: alt definition of norm and trace} we know that $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_i b_j)= \sum_k \sigma_k(b_i)\sigma_k(b_j)$ which is the same as the $(i,j)$ entry of $M^t M$. Therefore \[\det(T_B)=\det(M^t M)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: Trace is a sum over embeddings, so $T_B=M^tM$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a power basis
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ for some $\alpha \in K$. Then \[\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j} (\sigma_i(\alpha)-\sigma_j(\alpha))^2\] where $\sigma_i$ are the embeddings of $K $ into $\mathbb{C}$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ for some $\alpha \in K$.
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j} (\sigma_i(\alpha)-\sigma_j(\alpha))^2\] where $\sigma_i$ are the embeddings of $K $ into $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.label: prop: disc of prim elt basis

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First we recall a classical linear algebra result relating to the Vandermonde matrix, which states that \[\det \left (\begin{matrix} 1 & x_1& x_1^2&\cdots&x_1^{n-1} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n& x_n^2&\cdots&x_n^{n-1} \end{matrix} \right ) =\prod_{i<j} (x_i-x_j).\] Combining this with Proposition \ref{prop: disc via embs} gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Vandermonde determinant with the embedding formula.

nodes.name: Derivative of irreducible polynomial at a root
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$ and let $\alpha$ be one of its roots in $\mathbb{C}$. Then \[f'(\alpha)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (\alpha-\beta), \] where the product is over the roots of $f$ different from $\alpha$.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$ and let $\alpha$ be one of its roots in $\mathbb{C}$.
conclusions: \[f'(\alpha)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (\alpha-\beta), \] where the product is over the roots of $f$ different from $\alpha$.
nodes.label: lem: diff of irr pol

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We first write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$ which we can do (over $\mathbb{C}$) as $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, where now $g(x)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (x-\beta)$. Differentiating we get \[f'(x)=g(x)+(x-\alpha)g'(x).\] If we now evaluate at $\alpha$ we get the result.

nodes.name: Factor $f=(x-\alpha)g$
nodes.statement: We first write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$ which we can do (over $\mathbb{C}$) as $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, where now $g(x)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (x-\beta)$.

nodes.name: Product rule
nodes.statement: Differentiating we get \[f'(x)=g(x)+(x-\alpha)g'(x).\]

nodes.name: Evaluate at $\alpha$
nodes.statement: If we now evaluate at $\alpha$ we get the result.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a power basis via norm of derivative
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ and let $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$. Then \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))\] where $m_\alpha'$ is the derivative of $m_\alpha(x)$ (which we recall denotes the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$).
assumptions: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ and let $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$.
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))\] where $m_\alpha'$ is the derivative of $m_\alpha(x)$ (which we recall denotes the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$).
nodes.label: prop: num field disc in terms of norm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: disc of prim elt basis} we have $\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ where $\alpha_k:=\sigma_k(\alpha)$. Next, we note that the number of terms in this product is $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. So if we write each term as $(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=-(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)$ we get \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j). \] Now, by Lemma \ref{lem: diff of irr pol} and Proposition \ref{prop: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))=\prod_{i=1}^n m_\alpha'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j),\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the Vandermonde product with signs and recognize it as the norm of $m_\alpha'(\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Discriminant as product of squared differences
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: disc of prim elt basis} we have $\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ where $\alpha_k:=\sigma_k(\alpha)$.
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant as product of squared differences

nodes.name: Count terms to extract the sign
nodes.statement: Next, we note that the number of terms in this product is $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. So if we write each term as $(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=-(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)$ we get \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Count terms to extract the sign

nodes.name: Identify the product with $N(m_\alpha'(\alpha))$
nodes.statement: Now, by Lemma \ref{lem: diff of irr pol} and Proposition \ref{prop: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))=\prod_{i=1}^n m_\alpha'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j),\] which gives the result.

nodes.name: Discriminant of x^8-2
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $m_\alpha(x)=x^8-2$ (which is irreducible by Eisensteins criterion \ref{Eis crit}). Therefore $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ has degree $8$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ and a basis is $B:=\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^7\}$. From the above we then have \begin{align*}\Delta(B)= (-1)^{8\cdot7/2} N_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)/\mathbb{Q}} (m_\alpha'(\alpha))&= N_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)/\mathbb{Q}} (8\alpha^7)\\&=N_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)/\mathbb{Q}}(8) N_{\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha^7)=8^8 \cdot (-2)^7=-2^{31}\end{align*} Here we use that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha^7)=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^7$ and that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=-2$.
nodes.label: exmp: disc of x^8-2

nodes.name: Eisenstein elements give no new integers at p
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$and $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer such that $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisensteins Criterion \ref{Eis crit} for a prime $p$. Then none of the elements \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_0+x_1\alpha+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1})\] is an algebraic integer, where $n=\deg(m_\alpha)$ and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}.$
nodes.statement_short: If $m_\alpha$ is $p$-Eisenstein, no $\frac1p\sum x_i\alpha^i$ with digits $x_i$ is an algebraic integer.
assumptions: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$and $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer such that $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisensteins Criterion \ref{Eis crit} for a prime $p$.
conclusions: none of the elements \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_0+x_1\alpha+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1})\] is an algebraic integer, where $n=\deg(m_\alpha)$ and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}.$
nodes.label: lem: eis crit and alg ints

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We will only prove the case when $m_\alpha$ is Eisenstein, since the proof of the more general case is identical. Suppose for contradiction that $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and let $x_d$ be the first non-zero coefficient, so \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d+x_{d+1}\alpha^{d+1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Now, rewrite this as $\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d +\alpha^{d+1}\beta)$ for some $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Next, multiply through by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$, then we have \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\frac{\alpha^n\beta}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Now, since $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisenstein at $p$, we see that $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$ for some $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and therefore the above gives us that \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\beta f(\alpha) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] and thus \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Lets now calculate the norm of this: \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{n-1}}{p^n}.\] By Eisenstein the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is divisible by $p$ but not $p^2$, so since the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ we see that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=p a$ where $p \nmid a$. Therefore we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n p^{n-1}a^{n-1}}{p^n}= \frac{x_d^n a^{n-1}}{p}.\] But this cant be in $\mathbb{Z}$ since $p$ doesn't divide $x_d$ or $a$, and this gives us a contradiction since Proposition \ref{prop: norm trace of alg int is int} says that the norm of an algebraic integer must be an integer. So $\phi$ couldn't have been an algebraic integer.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: reduce to $x_d\alpha^{n-1}/p$ integral and compute its norm, which is not an integer.

nodes.name: Reduce to the Eisenstein case
nodes.statement: We will only prove the case when $m_\alpha$ is Eisenstein, since the proof of the more general case is identical.

nodes.name: Assume such $\phi$ is integral; take the first nonzero coefficient
nodes.statement: Suppose for contradiction that $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and let $x_d$ be the first non-zero coefficient, so \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d+x_{d+1}\alpha^{d+1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]
nodes.statement_short: Assume such $\phi$ is integral; take the first nonzero coefficient

nodes.name: Multiply by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$
nodes.statement: Now, rewrite this as $\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d +\alpha^{d+1}\beta)$ for some $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Next, multiply through by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$, then we have \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\frac{\alpha^n\beta}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]

nodes.name: Use $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: Now, since $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisenstein at $p$, we see that $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$ for some $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and therefore the above gives us that \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\beta f(\alpha) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] and thus \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]

nodes.name: Compute the norm
nodes.statement: Lets now calculate the norm of this: \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{n-1}}{p^n}.\]

nodes.name: $N(\alpha)=pa$ with $p\nmid a$
nodes.statement: By Eisenstein the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is divisible by $p$ but not $p^2$, so since the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ we see that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=p a$ where $p \nmid a$. Therefore we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n p^{n-1}a^{n-1}}{p^n}= \frac{x_d^n a^{n-1}}{p}.\]

nodes.name: Norm is not integral: contradiction
nodes.statement: But this cant be in $\mathbb{Z}$ since $p$ doesn't divide $x_d$ or $a$, and this gives us a contradiction since Proposition \ref{prop: norm trace of alg int is int} says that the norm of an algebraic integer must be an integer. So $\phi$ couldn't have been an algebraic integer.

nodes.name: Integral basis for x^8-2
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $x^8-2$. Then as we saw in Example \ref{exmp: disc of x^8-2} we know that $B=\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^7\}$ has discriminant $-2^{31}$. So the we only need to check at $p=2$. But $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisensteins criterion \ref{Eis crit} with $p=2$, therefore the Lemma \ref{lem: eis crit and alg ints} tells us that in fact this must be an integral basis, since dividing by $2$ wont ever give us new algebraic integers.

nodes.name: Degree invariant under Moebius transformation
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be an algebraic number with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$ and let $\beta \in \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be such that $\alpha=\frac{a}{b\beta+c}$ with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $b \neq 0$. Then $\deg(m_\alpha)=\deg(m_\beta)$.
assumptions: Let $\alpha$ be an algebraic number with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha$ and let $\beta \in \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be such that $\alpha=\frac{a}{b\beta+c}$ with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Q}$ and $b \neq 0$.
nodes.label: lem: min pol of lin trans

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)=\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$ (just do double inclusion). Then since $\deg(m_\beta)=[\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]=[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=\deg(m_\alpha)$ (by Cor. \ref{cor: min pol simple ext}) we get the result.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a trinomial
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ a number field with $m_\alpha(x)=x^n+ax+b$. Then \[\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\})=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}(n^nb^{n-1}+(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)^{n-1}a^n) .\]
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant of the power basis for $x^n+ax+b$.
assumptions: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ a number field with $m_\alpha(x)=x^n+ax+b$.
nodes.label: thm: disc of trinom

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: From Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm} we have \[\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))).\] Now, let $\beta=m_\alpha'(\alpha)$, then we have \[\beta=n \alpha^{n-1}+a=-(n-1)a-nb\alpha^{-1}.\] Since $\alpha^n+a\alpha+b=0$ implies $n\alpha^{n-1}=-na-nb\alpha^{-1}$. Which gives \[\alpha =\frac{-nb}{\beta+(n-1)a}.\] Now, using Lemma \ref{lem: min pol of lin trans} we see that $n=\deg(m_\alpha)=\deg(m_\beta)$. Moreover, if we take $m_\alpha(x)=x^n+ax+b$, evaluate at $\frac{-nb}{\beta+(n-1)a}$ and clear denominators, we get that \[(\beta+(n-1)a)^n-na(\beta+(n-1)a)^{n-1}+(-n)^nb^{n-1}=0.\] Therefore $\beta$ is a root of \[(x+(n-1)a)^n-na(x+(n-1)a)^{n-1}+(-n)^nb^{n-1}\] which is a monic polynomial of degree $n=\deg(m_\beta)$, therefore this is the minimal polynomial of $\beta$. Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: field pol min pol} or Corollary \ref{cor: field to min pol} we have $C_\beta=m_\beta$. Therefore by Proposition \ref{prop: field pol relation to norm and trace} we see that $(-1)^n$ times the constant coefficient of $m_\beta$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)$. Therefore we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)=n^nb^{n-1}+(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)^{n-1}a^n.\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $N(m_\alpha'(\alpha))$ by finding the minimal polynomial of $\beta=m_\alpha'(\alpha)$ and reading off its constant term.

nodes.name: Discriminant is $\pm N(m_\alpha'(\alpha))$
nodes.statement: From Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm} we have \[\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))).\]

nodes.name: Express $\alpha$ as a Moebius function of $\beta$
nodes.statement: Now, let $\beta=m_\alpha'(\alpha)$, then we have \[\beta=n \alpha^{n-1}+a=-(n-1)a-nb\alpha^{-1}.\] Since $\alpha^n+a\alpha+b=0$ implies $n\alpha^{n-1}=-na-nb\alpha^{-1}$. Which gives \[\alpha =\frac{-nb}{\beta+(n-1)a}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Express $\alpha$ as a Moebius function of $\beta$

nodes.name: $\deg m_\beta=n$
nodes.statement: Now, using Lemma \ref{lem: min pol of lin trans} we see that $n=\deg(m_\alpha)=\deg(m_\beta)$.

nodes.name: Find the minimal polynomial of $\beta$
nodes.statement: Moreover, if we take $m_\alpha(x)=x^n+ax+b$, evaluate at $\frac{-nb}{\beta+(n-1)a}$ and clear denominators, we get that \[(\beta+(n-1)a)^n-na(\beta+(n-1)a)^{n-1}+(-n)^nb^{n-1}=0.\] Therefore $\beta$ is a root of \[(x+(n-1)a)^n-na(x+(n-1)a)^{n-1}+(-n)^nb^{n-1}\] which is a monic polynomial of degree $n=\deg(m_\beta)$, therefore this is the minimal polynomial of $\beta$.

nodes.name: Read off the norm from the constant term
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: field pol min pol} or Corollary \ref{cor: field to min pol} we have $C_\beta=m_\beta$. Therefore by Proposition \ref{prop: field pol relation to norm and trace} we see that $(-1)^n$ times the constant coefficient of $m_\beta$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)$. Therefore we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)=n^nb^{n-1}+(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)^{n-1}a^n.\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Read off the norm from the constant term

nodes.name: Discriminant of a cubic field
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $m_\alpha(x)=x^3+ax+b$. Then \[\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2\})=-27b^2-4a^3.\]
assumptions: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $m_\alpha(x)=x^3+ax+b$.
nodes.label: cor: disc of cubic field

nodes.name: Reduction of cubic minimal polynomials
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ a number field with $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=3$. Then $m_\alpha(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ for $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Q}$. If we replace $\alpha$ with $\alpha':=\alpha+a/3$ then $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha')$ but this has the effect of removing the $x^2$ term in the minimal polynomial, so after relabelling if necessary, we have $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ with $m_{\alpha}(x)=x^3+ax+b$. Therefore Corollary \ref{cor: disc of cubic field} gives us a quick way to find the discriminant of a cubic field.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting $\alpha$ by $a/3$ removes the $x^2$ term, so the cubic-discriminant formula applies to every cubic field.

nodes.name: Ring of integers for x^3+x+1
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha$ be a root of $x^3+x+1$, and let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. Then $\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2\})=-31$ which is square-free and therefore by Corollary \ref{cor: square free implies int basis} $\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2\}$ is an integral basis and therefore $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Using Theorem \ref{thm: disc of trinom} show what if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d$ a square-free integer, then \[ \Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)= \begin{cases} d & \text{if } d \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \\ 4d & \text{if } d \equiv 2,3 \pmod 4. \\ \end{cases} \]
nodes.label: ques: disc of quad

nodes.name: Primitive n-th root of unity
nodes.statement: From now on, when we write $\zeta_n$ we mean a primitive $n$-root of unity, meaning $n$ is the smallest non-zero integer such that $\zeta_n^n=1$.

nodes.name: Minimal polynomial of zeta_p is Phi_p
nodes.statement: Lets look at the case $n=p$ for $p$ some prime number. Then from Example \ref{exp: cyclo min pol} we know that $x^p-1$ is not irreducible, but \[\Phi_p(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{p-1}\] is minimal. So $m_{\zeta_p}=\Phi_p$.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic polynomials are irreducible
nodes.statement: For $n$ any integer, $\Phi_n$ is an irreducible polynomial of degree $\varphi(n)$ (where $\varphi$ is Euler's Totient function).
nodes.label: lem: cyclo poly

nodes.name: Ring of integers of Q(zeta_p)
nodes.statement: Let $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime, let $\lambda_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Then $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$ moreover \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}p^{p-2}\]
assumptions: $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime, let $\lambda_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$
nodes.label: thm: ring of ints of cyclo

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: First note $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=p-1$. Since $\zeta_p=1-\lambda_p$ we at once get $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$ (just do double inclusion). Next, let $\alpha_i=\sigma_i(\zeta_p)$ denote the conjugates of $\zeta_p$, which is the same as the image of $\zeta_p$ under one of the embeddings $\sigma_i: \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p) \to \mathbb{C}$. Now by Proposition $\ref{prop: disc of prim elt basis}$ we have \begin{align*}\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\prod_{i < j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2 &=\prod_{i < j} ((1-\alpha_i)-(1-\alpha_j))^2\\&=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})\end{align*} Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm}, we have \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\cdots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )\] Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$. Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lambda_p}.\] Lastly, note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, from the computation in Example \ref{exp: cyclo min pol}, we see $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\lambda_p)=p$. Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)N_{K\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(-\lambda_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\] So the last thing we need to prove is that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. From the calculation we just did, the only prime dividing the discriminant is $p$, therefore Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} tells us the only prime we need to check is $p$. But from Lemma \ref{lem: eis crit and alg ints} we know that dividing by $p$ wont give us any new integral elements, so this must be an integral basis which give the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the discriminant via the norm of $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)$; only $p$ divides it, and the Eisenstein lemma rules out new integers at $p$.

nodes.name: Degree $p-1$
nodes.statement: First note $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=p-1$. Since $\zeta_p=1-\lambda_p$ we at once get $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$ (just do double inclusion).

nodes.name: Equal discriminants for both power bases
nodes.statement: Next, let $\alpha_i=\sigma_i(\zeta_p)$ denote the conjugates of $\zeta_p$, which is the same as the image of $\zeta_p$ under one of the embeddings $\sigma_i: \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p) \to \mathbb{C}$. Now by Proposition $\ref{prop: disc of prim elt basis}$ we have \begin{align*}\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\prod_{i < j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2 &=\prod_{i < j} ((1-\alpha_i)-(1-\alpha_j))^2\\&=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Equal discriminants for both power bases

nodes.name: Compute $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)$
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm}, we have \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\cdots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )\] Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$. Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lambda_p}.\]

nodes.name: Norms of $\zeta_p$, $\lambda_p$ give $p^{p-2}$
nodes.statement: Lastly, note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, from the computation in Example \ref{exp: cyclo min pol}, we see $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\lambda_p)=p$. Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)N_{K\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(-\lambda_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\]

nodes.name: Only $p$ to check; Eisenstein lemma finishes
nodes.statement: So the last thing we need to prove is that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. From the calculation we just did, the only prime dividing the discriminant is $p$, therefore Lemma \ref{lem: disc int basis} tells us the only prime we need to check is $p$. But from Lemma \ref{lem: eis crit and alg ints} we know that dividing by $p$ wont give us any new integral elements, so this must be an integral basis which give the result.
nodes.statement_short: Only $p$ to check; Eisenstein lemma finishes

nodes.name: Cyclotomic fields of prime power order
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Let $p$ be a prime, $k$ a positive integer and $\zeta_{p^k}$ be a $p^k$-th root of unity and let $\lambda_{p^k}=1-\zeta_{p^k}$. Show that \[\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{p^k}]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_{p^k}] \] and \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_{p^k},\dots,\zeta_{p^k}^{\varphi(p^k)}\})=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_{p^k},\dots,\lambda_{p^k}^{\varphi(p^k)}\}).\] Here $\varphi$ is the usual Euler totient function. \item Show that $\Delta(\{1,\zeta_{p^k},\dots,\zeta_{p^k}^{\varphi(p^k)}\})$ divides $p^{k\varphi(p^k)}$. \item Let $p$ be a prime and $n=p^k$. Let $S=\{1 \leq x \leq n \mid p\nmid x\}$ (i.e the set of elements less than $n$ which are not divisible by $p$). Show that \[\prod_{r \in S} (1-\zeta_{p^k}^r)=p\] and from this deduce that $\lambda_{p^k}^{\varphi(p^k)}$ divides $p$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{p^k}]$. [Hint: Consider the polynomial \[f(x)=\frac{x^{p^k}-1}{x^{p^{k-1}}-1}=1+x^{p^{k-1}}+x^{2p^{k-1}}+\cdots+x^{(p-1)p^{k-1}} \]] \item Using the above prove that if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{p^k})$ then $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{p^k}]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_{p^k}]$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Ring of integers of cyclotomic fields
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $\zeta_n$ a root of unity. If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ then \[\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n].\]
assumptions: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $\zeta_n$ a root of unity.
nodes.label: thm: ring of ints of cyclo field

nodes.name: Cyclotomic units
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\zeta_n$ be an $n$-th root of unity. Show that if $k$ is coprime to $n$ then \[1+\zeta_n+\cdots+\zeta_n^{k-1}\] is a unity in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n]$. [Hint:Check that its inverse is $\frac{1-\zeta_n}{1-\zeta_n^k}$]

nodes.name: p is a unit times (1-zeta)^phi(n)
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a prime and $n=p^k$. Show that \[p=u(1-\zeta_n)^{\varphi(n)}\] where $u \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n]^{\times}$ (i.e. $u$ is a unit).
nodes.label: ques: fac of p in p-th root

nodes.name: Units are elements of norm ±1
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ denote the group of units, then \[\mathcal{O}_K^\times=\{\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K \mid N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\pm 1\} \]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ denote the group of units,

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is a unit the $\alpha^{-1} \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{-1}=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha \alpha^{-1})=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(1)=1$. So $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) \in \mathbb{Z}^\times$ and is therefore $\pm 1$. Now, assume $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\pm 1$ and let $\sigma_i$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$ with $\sigma_1$ the identity embedding. Then \[\alpha \prod_{i=2}^n \sigma_i(\alpha)=\pm 1 \] which means $\alpha^{-1}=\pm \prod_{i=2}^n \sigma_i(\alpha)$ but each $\sigma_i(\alpha)$ is again an algebraic integer so $ \alpha^{-1} \in \overline{\mathbb{Z}} \cap K=\mathcal{O}_K$ (see Remark \ref{rmrk: all alg ints}).
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity of the norm for units; conversely the inverse is a product of conjugates, which are integral.

nodes.name: Units have norm $\pm1$
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is a unit the $\alpha^{-1} \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{-1}=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha \alpha^{-1})=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(1)=1$. So $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) \in \mathbb{Z}^\times$ and is therefore $\pm 1$.

nodes.name: Norm $\pm1$ gives an integral inverse
nodes.statement: Now, assume $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\pm 1$ and let $\sigma_i$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$ with $\sigma_1$ the identity embedding. Then \[\alpha \prod_{i=2}^n \sigma_i(\alpha)=\pm 1 \] which means $\alpha^{-1}=\pm \prod_{i=2}^n \sigma_i(\alpha)$ but each $\sigma_i(\alpha)$ is again an algebraic integer so $ \alpha^{-1} \in \overline{\mathbb{Z}} \cap K=\mathcal{O}_K$ (see Remark \ref{rmrk: all alg ints}).

nodes.name: 1+sqrt2 is a unit
nodes.statement: Let us look at $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$. In this case we have already seen that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{2}]$. Now, is $1+\sqrt{2}$ a unit? Well \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(1+\sqrt{2})=(1+\sqrt{2})(1-\sqrt{2})=-1\] So yes it is.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's Unit theorem
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let \[\mu_K=\{x \in K^\times \mid x^n=1 \text{ for some } n \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\}.\] This is the set of roots of unity in $K$. Let $r_1$ denote the number of real embeddings of $K$ and $r_2$ the number of complex conjugate pairs of embeddings. Then \[\mathcal{O}_K^{\times} \cong \mu_K \times \mathbb{Z}^{r_1+r_2-1}\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let \[\mu_K=\{x \in K^\times \mid x^n=1 \text{ for some } n \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}\}.\] This is the set of roots of unity in $K$. Let $r_1$ denote the number of real embeddings of $K$ and $r_2$ the number of complex conjugate pairs of embeddings.
nodes.label: thm: dir unit theorem

nodes.name: Units of imaginary quadratic fields
nodes.statement: If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ with $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$ a square-free integer, then $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ is $\mu_K$.
assumptions: If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$ with $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$ a square-free integer,

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: In this case $r_1=0$ and $r_2=1$ therefore Theorem \ref{thm: dir unit theorem} gives the result.

nodes.name: Roots of unity in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Show that if $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ a square-free integer, then \[ {\mu_K=} \begin{cases} \{\pm 1, \pm \sqrt{-1}\} & \text{if } d=-1\\ \{1, \zeta, \zeta^2, \zeta^3, \zeta^4, \zeta^5 \} & \text{if } d=-3\\ \{\pm 1\} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] where $\zeta=e^{2\pi/6}=\frac{1+\sqrt{-3}}{2}$.
nodes.label: ques: units in img quad

nodes.name: Units of real quadratic fields; fundamental unit
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d$ a positive square-free integer. Then \[\mathcal{O}_K^{\times} \cong \{\pm 1\} \times \mathbb{Z}.\] In this case there is a unique unit in $u \in \mathcal{O}_K^{\times}$ which generates $\mathcal{O}_K^\times/ \{\pm 1\}$ and under the standard embedding we have $u \geq 1$. This unit $u$ is called the fundamental unit.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{O}_K^\times\cong\{\pm1\}\times\mathbb{Z}$ for real quadratic $K$, generated by the fundamental unit $u>1$.
assumptions: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ with $d$ a positive square-free integer.
conclusions: \[\mathcal{O}_K^{\times} \cong \{\pm 1\} \times \mathbb{Z}.\] In this case there is a unique unit in $u \in \mathcal{O}_K^{\times}$ which generates $\mathcal{O}_K^\times/ \{\pm 1\}$ and under the standard embedding we have $u \geq 1$. This unit $u$ is called the fundamental unit.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Note that in this case $\mu_K=\{\pm 1\}$. So the structure of the group of units follows from Theorem \ref{thm: dir unit theorem}. Now, $\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}/\{\pm 1\} \cong \mathbb{Z}$ so take any unit $v$ mapping to a generator of $\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}/\{\pm 1\}$. Then one of $\{\pm v, \pm v^{-1}\}$ is in the set $(1,\infty)$. So let $u$ be this unit.
nodes.statement_short: Dirichlet's unit theorem with $\mu_K=\{\pm1\}$; normalize a generator to exceed 1.

nodes.name: Apply Dirichlet's unit theorem
nodes.statement: Note that in this case $\mu_K=\{\pm 1\}$. So the structure of the group of units follows from Theorem \ref{thm: dir unit theorem}.

nodes.name: Normalize a generator into $(1,\infty)$
nodes.statement: Now, $\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}/\{\pm 1\} \cong \mathbb{Z}$ so take any unit $v$ mapping to a generator of $\mathcal{O}_{K}^{\times}/\{\pm 1\}$. Then one of $\{\pm v, \pm v^{-1}\}$ is in the set $(1,\infty)$. So let $u$ be this unit.

nodes.name: Norm ±p implies irreducible
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$. If $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\pm p$ for $p$ a prime number, then $\alpha$ is an irreducible element of $\mathcal{O}_K$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha=\beta \gamma$ we want to show that one of $\beta,\gamma$ is a unit. Now taking norms we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)=\pm p. \] Therefore as $p$ is prime we must have $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)=\pm 1$ or $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)=\pm 1$. In either case we get the result.
nodes.statement_short: Norm is multiplicative, so a factorization of $\alpha$ forces a factor of norm $\pm1$.

nodes.name: Factor $\alpha=\beta\gamma$ and take norms
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha=\beta \gamma$ we want to show that one of $\beta,\gamma$ is a unit. Now taking norms we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)=\pm p. \]

nodes.name: One factor has norm $\pm1$, hence is a unit
nodes.statement: Therefore as $p$ is prime we must have $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)=\pm 1$ or $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)=\pm 1$. In either case we get the result.
nodes.statement_short: One factor has norm $\pm1$, hence is a unit

nodes.name: Converse fails: 3 in Z[i]
nodes.statement: The converse is false. For example in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-1}]$ the element $3$ is irreducible and has norm $9$.

nodes.name: Existence of factorization into irreducibles
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ be non-zero and not a unit. Then $\alpha$ can be written as a product of irreducible elements.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ be non-zero and not a unit.
conclusions: $\alpha$ can be written as a product of irreducible elements.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We prove this by induction on $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$. If $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=2$ then $\alpha$ is irreducible so we are done. Now assume it is true for all $\beta$ with $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)|< |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$. If $\alpha$ is irreducible then we are done, otherwise $\alpha=\beta \gamma$ with $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)|, |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)|< |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$. Therefore both $\beta$ and $\gamma$ can be factored into irreducibles and thus so can $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $|N(\alpha)|$: split a reducible element into factors of smaller norm.

nodes.name: Induction on the absolute norm
nodes.statement: We prove this by induction on $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: If $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=2$ then $\alpha$ is irreducible so we are done.

nodes.name: Inductive step: factor into smaller norms
nodes.statement: Now assume it is true for all $\beta$ with $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)|< |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$. If $\alpha$ is irreducible then we are done, otherwise $\alpha=\beta \gamma$ with $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)|, |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\gamma)|< |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$. Therefore both $\beta$ and $\gamma$ can be factored into irreducibles and thus so can $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: factor into smaller norms

nodes.name: Unique factorization
nodes.statement: We say a ring has unique factorization if whenever \[p_1p_2\cdots p_n=q_1q_2\cdots q_m\] for $p_i,q_i$ irreducible elements, then $n=m$ and after possibly reordering we can find units $u_i$ such that $p_i=u_iq_i$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Z[sqrt-10] lacks unique factorization
nodes.statement: The $\mathbb{Z}$ has unique factorization as does $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]$. But this is not usually the case, for example $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-10}]$ doesn't have unique factorization as $10=2 \cdot 5= -\sqrt{-10}\sqrt{-10}$ all of which are irreducible as can be seen by taking norms: Note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(2)=4,N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(5)=25, N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\sqrt{-10})=10$. Now, every element in $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-10})$ has norm of the form $x^2+10y^2$ and this can never be $\pm 2, \pm 5$, so there can't be any irreducible elements dividing $2,5,\sqrt{-10}$ therefore they are irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-2}]$ are UFDs; in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-10}]$, $10=2\cdot5=-\sqrt{-10}^2$ with irreducible factors.

nodes.name: Noetherian ring
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Then $R$ is called \textit{Noetherian} any of the following equivalent conditions holds: \begin{enumerate} \item Every ideal is finitely generated. \item Every increasing chain of ideals $I_1 \subset I_2 \subset \dots$ is eventually constant. \item Every non-empty set $S$ of ideals contains a (not necessarily unique) maximal member. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: definition: noeth ring

nodes.name: Equivalence of Noetherian conditions
nodes.statement: Check that these definitions are all equivalent.

nodes.name: O_K is Noetherian
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathcal{O}_K$ its ring of integers. Then $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a Noetherian ring.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathcal{O}_K$ its ring of integers.
nodes.label: prop: ring of ints is noeth

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We saw in Corollary \ref{cor: int basis exists} that $\mathcal{O}_K$ is finitely generated as an additive group. Now, any ideal $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ is an additive subgroup of the \textit{abelian} group $\mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore is also finitely generated.\footnote{Be warned, its not true in general that a subgroup of a finitely generated group $G$ is finitely generated. You really need $G$ to be abelian for this to work.} So $\mathcal{O}_K$ is Noetherian.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a finitely generated abelian group, so its ideals are finitely generated.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{O}_K$ is finitely generated additively
nodes.statement: We saw in Corollary \ref{cor: int basis exists} that $\mathcal{O}_K$ is finitely generated as an additive group.

nodes.name: Subgroups of f.g. abelian groups are f.g.
nodes.statement: Now, any ideal $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ is an additive subgroup of the \textit{abelian} group $\mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore is also finitely generated.\footnote{Be warned, its not true in general that a subgroup of a finitely generated group $G$ is finitely generated. You really need $G$ to be abelian for this to work.} So $\mathcal{O}_K$ is Noetherian.
nodes.statement_short: Subgroups of f.g. abelian groups are f.g.

nodes.name: Nonzero ideals contain integers and have finite quotient
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a}$ a non-zero ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$. Then $\mathfrak{a}$ contains some positive integer and moreover the quotient ring $\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{a}$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero ideal contains the norm of any nonzero element, and $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$ is finite.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a}$ a non-zero ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$.
conclusions: $\mathfrak{a}$ contains some positive integer and moreover the quotient ring $\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{a}$ is finite.
nodes.label: prop: quot of ideal is finite

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a} \backslash 0$ and $N=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$. Since $\alpha \neq 0$, then $N \neq 0$. Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that $N=\alpha \beta$ where $\beta$ is a product of conjugates of $\alpha$ so it is in $\overline{\mathbb{Z}}$. Moreover, $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$ since $\beta=N/\alpha \in K$ (recall $\mathcal{O}_K=K \cap \overline{\mathbb{Z}}$). But since $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal $N=\alpha \beta \in \mathfrak{a}$. Now, lets use this to prove the quotient is finite. First note that since $N \in \mathfrak{a}$ then $(N) \subset \mathfrak{a}$ therefore $|\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{a}| \leq |\mathcal{O}_K / (N)|$. Secondly, since $\mathcal{O}_K$ is finitely generated as an abelian group, by picking an integral basis we get an isomorphism (of additive abelian groups) $\mathcal{O}_K \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$ where $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/(N) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^n$ which is finite. Therefore so is $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: $N(\alpha)=\alpha\beta\in\mathfrak{a}$ with $\beta$ integral; then $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$ is a quotient of $(\mathbb{Z}/N)^n$.

nodes.name: Take $N=N(\alpha)\neq 0$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a} \backslash 0$ and $N=N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$. Since $\alpha \neq 0$, then $N \neq 0$.

nodes.name: $N=\alpha\beta$ with $\beta\in\mathcal{O}_K$, so $N\in\mathfrak{a}$
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that $N=\alpha \beta$ where $\beta$ is a product of conjugates of $\alpha$ so it is in $\overline{\mathbb{Z}}$. Moreover, $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$ since $\beta=N/\alpha \in K$ (recall $\mathcal{O}_K=K \cap \overline{\mathbb{Z}}$). But since $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal $N=\alpha \beta \in \mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Now prove finiteness
nodes.statement: Now, lets use this to prove the quotient is finite.

nodes.name: $|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}|\le|\mathcal{O}_K/(N)|$
nodes.statement: First note that since $N \in \mathfrak{a}$ then $(N) \subset \mathfrak{a}$ therefore $|\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{a}| \leq |\mathcal{O}_K / (N)|$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{O}_K/(N)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/N)^n$ is finite
nodes.statement: Secondly, since $\mathcal{O}_K$ is finitely generated as an abelian group, by picking an integral basis we get an isomorphism (of additive abelian groups) $\mathcal{O}_K \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$ where $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/(N) \cong (\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^n$ which is finite. Therefore so is $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Finite integral domains are fields
nodes.statement: A finite integral domain is a field.
assumptions: A finite integral domain
nodes.label: lem: fin int dom is field

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a finite, non-trivial integral domain. Let $r \in R\backslash 0$. We need to show that $r$ has an inverse. Here is the trick: consider the sequence $r,r^2,r^3,\dots.$ Since $R$ is finite at some point we must have $r^n=r^m$ for some $m<n$. Then $r^m(r^{n-m}-1)=0$, but this is where being an integral domain comes in, since this means either $r^m=0$ or $r^{n-m}-1=0$. Since $r \neq 0$ and $R$ is an integral domain $r^m \neq 0$. Therefore $r^{n-m}=1$. This means $r^{-1}=r^{n-m-1}$ and therefore $r$ has an inverse.
nodes.statement_short: Powers of $r$ repeat in a finite ring; cancellation gives $r^{n-m}=1$.

nodes.name: Fix nonzero $r$; need an inverse
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a finite, non-trivial integral domain. Let $r \in R\backslash 0$. We need to show that $r$ has an inverse.

nodes.name: Consider the powers of $r$
nodes.statement: Here is the trick: consider the sequence $r,r^2,r^3,\dots.$

nodes.name: Two powers coincide
nodes.statement: Since $R$ is finite at some point we must have $r^n=r^m$ for some $m<n$.

nodes.name: Factor the difference
nodes.statement: Then $r^m(r^{n-m}-1)=0$, but this is where being an integral domain comes in, since this means either $r^m=0$ or $r^{n-m}-1=0$.

nodes.name: Cancellation gives $r^{n-m}=1$
nodes.statement: Since $r \neq 0$ and $R$ is an integral domain $r^m \neq 0$. Therefore $r^{n-m}=1$. This means $r^{-1}=r^{n-m-1}$ and therefore $r$ has an inverse.

nodes.name: Nonzero prime ideals of O_K are maximal
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field. Then every non-zero prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ is maximal.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field.
conclusions: every non-zero prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ is maximal.
nodes.label: cor: prim ideal is maximal

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings} we know that if $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ is a prime ideal then $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ is an integral domain. Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: quot of ideal is finite} $\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{p}$ is finite. But by Lemma \ref{lem: fin int dom is field} this is then a field. Now, using Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings} again, $\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ is a finite integral domain, hence a field.

nodes.name: Quotient is an integral domain
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings} we know that if $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ is a prime ideal then $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ is an integral domain.

nodes.name: Quotient is finite
nodes.statement: Now, by Proposition \ref{prop: quot of ideal is finite} $\mathcal{O}_K /\mathfrak{p}$ is finite.

nodes.name: Finite domain is a field
nodes.statement: But by Lemma \ref{lem: fin int dom is field} this is then a field.

nodes.name: So $\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal
nodes.statement: Now, using Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings} again, $\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal.

nodes.name: Integral elements, integral closure, integrally closed
nodes.statement: Let $R,A$ be rings with $A \subset R$ a subring and $x \in R$. We say $x$ is integral over $A$ if there exist $a_i \in A$ such that \[x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0=0\] for some $n$. Let $A'$ be the set of all elements of $R$ that are integral over $A$. Then similarly to how we prove Corollary \ref{cor: sum and mult of alg ints is alg ints}, $A'$ is a ring which we call the integral closure of $A$ in $R$. Moreover, if $R$ is an integral domain and we let \[\mathrm{Frac}(R):=\{a/b | a,b \in R, b \neq 0\}\] be its fields of fractions (this can alternatively be defined as smallest field containing $R$), then we say $R$ is integrally closed, if it is integrally closed in its field of fractions.

nodes.name: Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: A Dedekind domain is an integral domain $R$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $R$ is Noetherian. \item Every non-zero prime ideal is maximal. \item $R$ is integrally closed. \end{enumerate}
differentia: Every non-zero prime ideal is maximal.
nodes.label: definition: ded dom

nodes.name: O_K is a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$. Then $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a Dedekind domain.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: ring of ints is noeth} we get $(1)$ and by Corollary \ref{cor: prim ideal is maximal} we get $(2)$. So we only need to prove $\mathcal{O}_K$ is integrally closed. Let $\gamma=\alpha / \beta \in K$ satisfy a monic polynomial with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_K$, then I claim that it is in fact an algebraic integer and therefore it is in $K \cap \overline{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathcal{O}_K$. (Note $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_K)=K$.) The claim is Exercise \ref{quest: ints in tower law}.
nodes.statement_short: Noetherian and dimension one from earlier results; integral closedness from the integrality exercise.

nodes.name: Conditions (1) and (2) from earlier results
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: ring of ints is noeth} we get $(1)$ and by Corollary \ref{cor: prim ideal is maximal} we get $(2)$.

nodes.name: Remains: integrally closed
nodes.statement: So we only need to prove $\mathcal{O}_K$ is integrally closed.

nodes.name: Claim: such $\gamma$ is an algebraic integer
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma=\alpha / \beta \in K$ satisfy a monic polynomial with coefficients in $\mathcal{O}_K$, then I claim that it is in fact an algebraic integer and therefore it is in $K \cap \overline{\mathbb{Z}}=\mathcal{O}_K$. (Note $\mathrm{Frac}(\mathcal{O}_K)=K$.)
nodes.statement_short: Claim: such $\gamma$ is an algebraic integer

nodes.name: The claim is an exercise
nodes.statement: The claim is Exercise \ref{quest: ints in tower law}.

nodes.name: Ideals of a Dedekind domain contain products of primes
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain. Then every ideal contains a product of prime ideals.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain.
conclusions: every ideal contains a product of prime ideals.
nodes.label: lem: ded dom ideal has prim ideals

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Assume for contradiction this is not the case. Let $S$ denote the set of all ideals that do not contain a product of prime ideals. Then, since $R$ is Noetherian, by Definition \ref{definition: noeth ring}$(3)$, $S$ must contain a maximal element $\mathfrak{m}$ (not to be confused with maximal ideal, here maximal means with respect to the property of not containing a product of prime ideals). Now $\mathfrak{m}$ cannot be prime (otherwise $\mathfrak{m} \subseteq \mathfrak{m}$ gives a contradiction). Therefore we can find $r,s \in R \backslash \mathfrak{m}$ such that $rs \in \mathfrak{m}$. Now the ideals $(r)+\mathfrak{m}$ and $(s)+\mathfrak{m}$ are both larger then $\mathfrak{m}$ so must contain a product of prime ideals, but then so does their product $((r)+\mathfrak{m})((s)+\mathfrak{m})$. This product is contained in $\mathfrak{m}$ (since $rs \in \mathfrak{m}$) so we have a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Noetherian maximal counterexample $\mathfrak{m}$ is not prime; enlarging by $r,s$ gives a product of primes inside $\mathfrak{m}$.

nodes.name: Assume a counterexample exists
nodes.statement: Assume for contradiction this is not the case.

nodes.name: Take a maximal counterexample $\mathfrak{m}$
nodes.statement: Let $S$ denote the set of all ideals that do not contain a product of prime ideals. Then, since $R$ is Noetherian, by Definition \ref{definition: noeth ring}$(3)$, $S$ must contain a maximal element $\mathfrak{m}$ (not to be confused with maximal ideal, here maximal means with respect to the property of not containing a product of prime ideals).

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{m}$ is not prime
nodes.statement: Now $\mathfrak{m}$ cannot be prime (otherwise $\mathfrak{m} \subseteq \mathfrak{m}$ gives a contradiction).

nodes.name: Pick $r,s\notin\mathfrak{m}$ with $rs\in\mathfrak{m}$
nodes.statement: Therefore we can find $r,s \in R \backslash \mathfrak{m}$ such that $rs \in \mathfrak{m}$.

nodes.name: Larger ideals contain prime products
nodes.statement: Now the ideals $(r)+\mathfrak{m}$ and $(s)+\mathfrak{m}$ are both larger then $\mathfrak{m}$ so must contain a product of prime ideals, but then so does their product $((r)+\mathfrak{m})((s)+\mathfrak{m})$.

nodes.name: Their product lies in $\mathfrak{m}$: contradiction
nodes.statement: This product is contained in $\mathfrak{m}$ (since $rs \in \mathfrak{m}$) so we have a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proper ideals have fractional multipliers
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with field of fractions $K$ and $\mathfrak{a}$ a proper ideal . Then there is an element $x \in K \backslash R$ such that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$.
nodes.statement_short: For a proper ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ there is $x\in K\setminus R$ with $x\mathfrak{a}\subset R$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain with field of fractions $K$ and $\mathfrak{a}$ a proper ideal .
conclusions: there is an element $x \in K \backslash R$ such that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$.
nodes.label: lem: proper ideal mult by frac is still int

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ be any non-zero element. By Lemma \ref{lem: ded dom ideal has prim ideals} the ideal $(a)$ contains a product of prime ideals. So lets take prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_i$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^m \mathfrak{p}_i \subset (a)$ with $m$ as small as possible. Now, since every proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ (see Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings}), which is also a prime ideal (as maximal ideals are always prime). Therefore $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{p}$, so $\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i \subset \mathfrak{p}$. Now $\mathfrak{p}$ must contain some $\mathfrak{p}_i$ since if not, we can take $a_i \in \mathfrak{p}_i \backslash \mathfrak{p}$ then $\mathfrak{p}$ contains $\prod_i a_i$ but none of the $a_i$ which contradicts $\mathfrak{p}$ being a prime ideal. So after possibly relabelling we have $\mathfrak{p}_1 \subset \mathfrak{p}$. But by Definition \ref{definition: ded dom}, in a Dedekind domain all prime ideals are maximal, so $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}_1$. Since $m$ was taken as small as possible, $(a)$ can't contain any smaller product of prime ideals, so we can find $b \in (\prod_{i=2}^m \mathfrak{p}_i) \backslash (a)$. We claim that taking $x=\frac{b}{a}$ gives the result: First note $x \in K \backslash R$ since otherwise $\frac{b}{a}=c \in R$ therefore $b=ac \in (a)$ which contradicts our choice of $b$. Moreover, we claim that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$. To see this note that since $b \mathfrak{p} \subset \prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i \subset (a)$ we have $x \mathfrak{p} \subset R$ and therefore since $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we have $x\mathfrak{a} \subset x\mathfrak{p} \subset R$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a minimal product of primes in $(a)$, one equal to the maximal $\mathfrak{p}\supset\mathfrak{a}$; then $x=b/a$ with $b$ in the remaining product works.

nodes.name: Minimal product of primes inside $(a)$
nodes.statement: Let $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ be any non-zero element. By Lemma \ref{lem: ded dom ideal has prim ideals} the ideal $(a)$ contains a product of prime ideals. So lets take prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_i$ such that $\prod_{i=1}^m \mathfrak{p}_i \subset (a)$ with $m$ as small as possible.

nodes.name: Choose a maximal $\mathfrak{p}\supset\mathfrak{a}$
nodes.statement: Now, since every proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ (see Proposition \ref{prop: prime and max ideals in rings}), which is also a prime ideal (as maximal ideals are always prime). Therefore $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{p}$, so $\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i \subset \mathfrak{p}$.

So after possibly relabelling we have $\mathfrak{p}_1 \subset \mathfrak{p}$. But by Definition \ref{definition: ded dom}, in a Dedekind domain all prime ideals are maximal, so $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}_1$.

nodes.name: Claim: $x=b/a$ works
nodes.statement: We claim that taking $x=\frac{b}{a}$ gives the result: First note $x \in K \backslash R$ since otherwise $\frac{b}{a}=c \in R$ therefore $b=ac \in (a)$ which contradicts our choice of $b$. Moreover, we claim that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$. To see this note that since $b \mathfrak{p} \subset \prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i \subset (a)$ we have $x \mathfrak{p} \subset R$ and therefore since $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we have $x\mathfrak{a} \subset x\mathfrak{p} \subset R$.
