nodes.name: $x\mathfrak{a}\subset R$
nodes.statement: Moreover, we claim that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$. To see this note that since $b \mathfrak{p} \subset \prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i \subset (a)$ we have $x \mathfrak{p} \subset R$ and therefore since $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we have $x\mathfrak{a} \subset x\mathfrak{p} \subset R$.

nodes.name: Every ideal has a principal multiple
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a}$ an ideal in $R$. Then there is an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}$ is principal.
nodes.statement_short: For every ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ of a Dedekind domain there is $\mathfrak{b}$ with $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ principal.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a}$ an ideal in $R$.
conclusions: there is an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}$ is principal.
nodes.label: thm: ideals are invertible

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a} \backslash 0$ and let \[\mathfrak{b}=\{\beta \in R \mid \beta \mathfrak{a} \in (\alpha)\}.\] This is again an ideal and it is non-zero since $\alpha \neq 0$. By definition we have \begin{equation} \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} \subset (\alpha) \tag{$\dagger$}\end{equation} so we need to show equality. For this consider the set $\mathfrak{c}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}$. This is a subset of $R$ by $(\dagger)$ and is in fact an ideal. Now, if $\mathfrak{c}=R$ then $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}=(\alpha)$ and we are done. So assume for contradiction that $\mathfrak{c}$ is a proper ideal. Then by Lemma \ref{lem: proper ideal mult by frac is still int} we can find $x \in K \backslash R$ with $K$ the fraction field of $R$ and $x \mathfrak{c} \subset R$. Next, we note that $\mathfrak{c}$ contains $\mathfrak{b}$ since $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$, therefore $x \mathfrak{b} \subset x \mathfrak{c} \subset R$. Moreover, since $x\mathfrak{c}=\frac{x}{\alpha}\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{a} \subset R$ we have $x\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{a} \subset (\alpha)$. Now, if we look back at the definition of $\mathfrak{b}$ we see that since $x \mathfrak{b} \subset R$ we have $x\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{b}$. If we let $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n$ be a generating set for $\mathfrak{b}$, we can use $x\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{b}$ to think of multiplication by $x$ on $\mathfrak{b}$ as a matrix $A_x$ defined by \[x (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)^t=A_x (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)^t.\] $A_x$ is a $n \times n$ matrix over $R$ which has $x$ as an eigenvalue. This means, $x$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R$. But $R$ is integrally closed, so $x \in R$ which gives a contradiction as we took $x \in K\backslash R$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Set $\mathfrak{b}=(\alpha):\mathfrak{a}$; if $\frac1\alpha\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ were proper, the lemma gives $x\notin R$ stabilizing $\mathfrak{b}$, hence integral, contradiction.

nodes.name: Define $\mathfrak{b}$; then $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\subset(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a} \backslash 0$ and let \[\mathfrak{b}=\{\beta \in R \mid \beta \mathfrak{a} \in (\alpha)\}.\] This is again an ideal and it is non-zero since $\alpha \neq 0$. By definition we have \begin{equation} \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} \subset (\alpha) \tag{$\dagger$}\end{equation} so we need to show equality.

nodes.name: Consider $\mathfrak{c}=\frac1\alpha\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$
nodes.statement: For this consider the set $\mathfrak{c}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}$. This is a subset of $R$ by $(\dagger)$ and is in fact an ideal. Now, if $\mathfrak{c}=R$ then $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}=(\alpha)$ and we are done.

nodes.name: If $\mathfrak{c}$ proper, get $x\notin R$ with $x\mathfrak{c}\subset R
nodes.statement: So assume for contradiction that $\mathfrak{c}$ is a proper ideal. Then by Lemma \ref{lem: proper ideal mult by frac is still int} we can find $x \in K \backslash R$ with $K$ the fraction field of $R$ and $x \mathfrak{c} \subset R$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathfrak{c}$ proper, get $x\notin R$ with $x\mathfrak{c}\subset R$

nodes.name: $x\mathfrak{b}\subset\mathfrak{b}$
nodes.statement: Next, we note that $\mathfrak{c}$ contains $\mathfrak{b}$ since $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$, therefore $x \mathfrak{b} \subset x \mathfrak{c} \subset R$. Moreover, since $x\mathfrak{c}=\frac{x}{\alpha}\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{a} \subset R$ we have $x\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{a} \subset (\alpha)$. Now, if we look back at the definition of $\mathfrak{b}$ we see that since $x \mathfrak{b} \subset R$ we have $x\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{b}$.

nodes.name: $x$ is integral over $R$, contradiction
nodes.statement: If we let $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n$ be a generating set for $\mathfrak{b}$, we can use $x\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{b}$ to think of multiplication by $x$ on $\mathfrak{b}$ as a matrix $A_x$ defined by \[x (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)^t=A_x (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_n)^t.\] $A_x$ is a $n \times n$ matrix over $R$ which has $x$ as an eigenvalue. This means, $x$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $R$. But $R$ is integrally closed, so $x \in R$ which gives a contradiction as we took $x \in K\backslash R$. This completes the proof.

nodes.name: a b contained in (alpha)
nodes.statement: \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} \subset (\alpha) \tag{$\dagger$}

nodes.name: Principal multiple implies principal
nodes.statement: Show that if $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal in an integral domain $R$ and $(\alpha)\mathfrak{a}$ is principal for $\alpha \in R \backslash{0}$, then $\mathfrak{a}$ is principal.
nodes.label: ques: if prod is princ, you are princ

nodes.name: Fractional ideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $K$ its field of fractions. A \textit{fractional ideal} is a subset $\mathfrak{a} \subset K$ such that \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathfrak{a}$ is an abelian group under addition. \item $x \mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{a}$ for every $x \in R$. \item There exists some $x \in R$ such that $x\mathfrak{a} \subset R$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Examples of fractional ideals
nodes.statement: Let $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, then \[(q)=\{nq \mid n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\] is a fractional ideal. More generally, if $R$ is an Dedekind domain $K$ its field of fractions and $\alpha \subset K$. Then for any ideal $\mathfrak{a} \in R$, $\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal.

nodes.name: Fractional ideals are not closed under products of elements
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal and $x,y \in \mathfrak{a}$ then it is not necessarily true that $xy \in \mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Principal fractional ideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind ring and $K$ its field of fractions. For each $x \in K$ we call the fractional ideal \[(x)=\{xy\mid y \in R\}\] a \textit{principal fractional ideal}.
nodes.label: definition: princ frac ideal

nodes.name: Fractional ideals form a group
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $K$ its field of fractions. Then the set $J_K$ of non-zero fractional ideals forms a group under multiplication with $(1)=R$ being the identity.
nodes.statement_short: Nonzero fractional ideals of a Dedekind domain form a group $J_K$ with identity $R$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and $K$ its field of fractions.
conclusions: the set $J_K$ of non-zero fractional ideals forms a group under multiplication with $(1)=R$ being the identity.
nodes.label: prop: frac ideals form grp

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: As we had before, if $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ are fractional ideals, then $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ is defined as the fractional ideal generated by products of elements in $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$. This is clearly associative, so we only need to check the existence of inverses. If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a proper ideal of $R$, then by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} we can find an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} =(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$. Then setting $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{b}$ gives an inverse to $\mathfrak{a}$. If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal, then we can find some $x \in R$ such that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$ is an ideal (not just a fractional ideal), call it $\mathfrak{c}$, then $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=x\mathfrak{c}^{-1}$ is the inverse.
nodes.statement_short: Inverses: for an ideal use a principal multiple; for a fractional ideal scale into $R$ first.

nodes.name: Multiplication is associative; need inverses
nodes.statement: As we had before, if $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ are fractional ideals, then $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$ is defined as the fractional ideal generated by products of elements in $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$. This is clearly associative, so we only need to check the existence of inverses.

nodes.name: Inverse of an integral ideal
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a proper ideal of $R$, then by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} we can find an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} =(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha$. Then setting $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{b}$ gives an inverse to $\mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Inverse of a fractional ideal
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal, then we can find some $x \in R$ such that $x \mathfrak{a} \subset R$ is an ideal (not just a fractional ideal), call it $\mathfrak{c}$, then $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=x\mathfrak{c}^{-1}$ is the inverse.

nodes.name: Inverse fractional ideal formula
nodes.statement: It follows, that if $\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal in $R$, then \[\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=\{x \in K | x\mathfrak{a} \subset R \}\] where $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$.

nodes.name: Cancellation of ideals
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{c}$ are non-zero ideals in a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{c}$ then $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{c}$.
assumptions: If $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{c}$ are non-zero ideals in a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{c}$
nodes.label: cor: cancel of ideals

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Multiplying on the left by $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}$ gives the result.

nodes.name: To contain is to divide
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be ideals in a Dedekind domain. Then $\mathfrak{a} \mid \mathfrak{b}$ if and only if\/ $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}$.
assumptions: $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be ideals in a Dedekind domain
nodes.label: cor: ideal div

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a} \mid \mathfrak{b}$ then by definition we have $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{c} \mathfrak{a}$, which means $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}$. Conversely, assume that $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}$. Then by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} we can find an ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ such that $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}=(\alpha)$. Now, $\mathfrak{m} \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}=(\alpha)$ therefore $\mathfrak{c}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{m} \mathfrak{b}$ is again in $R$ and moreover it is an ideal (since, for example it is the product of two fractional ideals). The result follows from then noting that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$.
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility gives containment; conversely use a principal multiple $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}=(\alpha)$ to build $\mathfrak{c}$.

nodes.name: Divides implies contains
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a} \mid \mathfrak{b}$ then by definition we have $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{c} \mathfrak{a}$, which means $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Contains implies divides via $\mathfrak{c}=\frac1\alpha\mathfrak{m}\ma
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}$. Then by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} we can find an ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ such that $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}=(\alpha)$. Now, $\mathfrak{m} \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{m}=(\alpha)$ therefore $\mathfrak{c}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\mathfrak{m} \mathfrak{b}$ is again in $R$ and moreover it is an ideal (since, for example it is the product of two fractional ideals). The result follows from then noting that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$.

nodes.name: Unique factorization of ideals in Dedekind domains
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain, then every ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ can be written uniquely as a product of prime ideals, i.e, \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\dots\mathfrak{p}_n,\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i$ prime ideals (not necessarily distinct).
nodes.statement_short: Every ideal of a Dedekind domain is uniquely a product of prime ideals.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain,
conclusions: every ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ can be written uniquely as a product of prime ideals, i.e, \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\dots\mathfrak{p}_n,\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i$ prime ideals (not necessarily distinct).
nodes.label: thm: ded dom ideal is prod of prim

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Lets begin by showing that every ideal can be written as a product of prime ideal. Assume for contradiction that this is not the case. Then the set of proper ideals which are not a product of prime ideals, must have a maximal element by Definition \ref{definition: noeth ring} $(3)$. Let $\mathfrak{b}$ be this maximal element. Then $\mathfrak{b}$ must be contained in some maximal ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $R$ (which we recall is also prime). Then by Corollary \ref{cor: ideal div} we have $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{p} \mathfrak{c}$. This implies $\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{c}$ and this must be a strict containment as otherwise if $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$ then $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{p}$ which by Corollary \ref{cor: cancel of ideals} would mean $\mathfrak{p}=R$, which cannot happen as $\mathfrak{p}$ is a proper ideal. Now, since $\mathfrak{c}$ is larger than $\mathfrak{b}$ we must have $\mathfrak{c}$ being a product of prime ideals. So then $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$ is also a product of prime ideals contradicting our assumption. Lets now prove that the representation as a product of prime ideals is unique. Suppose we have \[\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\dots\mathfrak{p}_n=\mathfrak{q}_1\mathfrak{q}_2\dots\mathfrak{q}_m\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i,\mathfrak{q}_i$ not necessarily distinct prime ideals. Then $\mathfrak{q}_1\dots\mathfrak{q}_m \subset \mathfrak{p}_1$, which means $\mathfrak{p}_1$ contains some $\mathfrak{q}_i$ (see the proof of Lemma \ref{lem: proper ideal mult by frac is still int} to see why this is true). By relabelling the $\mathfrak{q}_i$ we can assume $\mathfrak{q}_1 \subset \mathfrak{p}_1$. But since all prime ideals in a Dedekind ring are maximal we must have $\mathfrak{q}_1=\mathfrak{p}_1$. So we can cancel this from each side of the equality to get \[\mathfrak{p}_2\dots\mathfrak{p}_n=\mathfrak{q}_2\dots\mathfrak{q}_m.\] Continuing like this we get $n=m$ and after relabelling $\mathfrak{p}_i=\mathfrak{q}_i$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Existence via a maximal counterexample and cancellation; uniqueness by peeling off equal primes.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: Lets now prove that the representation as a product of prime ideals is unique. Suppose we have \[\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\dots\mathfrak{p}_n=\mathfrak{q}_1\mathfrak{q}_2\dots\mathfrak{q}_m\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i,\mathfrak{q}_i$ not necessarily distinct prime ideals. nodes.name: Prime factorization with exponents
nodes.statement: Since ideal multiplication commutes, we usually write the factorization of a an ideal as \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_1^{e_1}\mathfrak{p}_2^{e_1}\dots\mathfrak{p}_r^{e_r}\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i$ distinct prime ideals.

nodes.name: Unique factorization of ideals in O_K
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field. Then every ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ can factored uniquely into a product of prime ideals.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field.
conclusions: every ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ can factored uniquely into a product of prime ideals.

nodes.name: gcd and lcm of ideals
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be ideals. Then we define the greatest common divisor $\gcd$ and least common multiple $\mathrm{lcm}$ as follows: Let $\mathfrak{a}=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}$ and $\mathfrak{b}=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{m_i}$ then \[\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{\min(n_i,m_i)} \qquad \mathrm{lcm}(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{\max(n_i,m_i)}.\] Here the $\mathfrak{p}_i$ are all different.
nodes.label: definition: ideal gcd and lcm

nodes.name: gcd is sum, lcm is intersection
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ are ideals. Then \[\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\] and \[\mathrm{lcm}(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}\]
assumptions: If $R$ is a Dedekind domain and $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ are ideals.
nodes.label: prop: ideal gcd and lcm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor: ideal div} tells us that division turns into containment for ideals, so the greatest common divisor of $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ is the smallest ideal containing both $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ which by definition is $\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}$. Similarly, the least common multiple is the largest ideal contained in both of them, which by definition is $\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$.
nodes.statement_short: Divisibility is containment, so gcd is the smallest containing ideal and lcm the largest contained.

nodes.name: gcd times lcm
nodes.statement: Show that $\gcd(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})\mathrm{lcm}(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b})=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$.
nodes.label: ques: ideal gcd lcm

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be coprime ideals (i.e., $\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=(1)$) then \[R/\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b} \cong R/\mathfrak{a} \times R/\mathfrak{b}\]
assumptions: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be coprime ideals (i.e., $\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=(1)$)
nodes.label: thm: chinese rem theorem

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Consider the ring homomorphism \[\phi: R \to R/\mathfrak{a} \times R/\mathfrak{b}\] given by $\phi(x)=(x \pmod \mathfrak{a}, x \pmod \mathfrak{b})$. Then the kernel is given by $\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$. Now, since $\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=(1)$ then \[\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b} =(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b})=(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{a})+(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{b}) \subset \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}.\] Moreover, its easy to see $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$, therefore $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$. So we have an injective ring homomorphism \[\phi':R/ \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=R/(\mathfrak{a}\cap \mathfrak{b}) \longrightarrow R/\mathfrak{a} \times R/\mathfrak{b}.\] It remains to check it is surjective. Write $1=a+b$ for $a \in \mathfrak{a},b \in \mathfrak{b}$, then for any $(r,s) \in R^2$ the element $x=as+br \in R$ is such that $x \equiv r \pmod \mathfrak{a}$ and $x \equiv s \pmod \mathfrak{b}$ which gives us subjectivity.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction map has kernel $\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$; surjective via $1=a+b$.

nodes.name: Reduction map with kernel $\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}$
nodes.statement: Consider the ring homomorphism \[\phi: R \to R/\mathfrak{a} \times R/\mathfrak{b}\] given by $\phi(x)=(x \pmod \mathfrak{a}, x \pmod \mathfrak{b})$. Then the kernel is given by $\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$.

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}$, injectivity
nodes.statement: Now, since $\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=(1)$ then \[\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b} =(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b})=(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{a})+(\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b})(\mathfrak{b}) \subset \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b}.\] Moreover, its easy to see $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$, therefore $\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a} \cap \mathfrak{b}$. So we have an injective ring homomorphism \[\phi':R/ \mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}=R/(\mathfrak{a}\cap \mathfrak{b}) \longrightarrow R/\mathfrak{a} \times R/\mathfrak{b}.\]

nodes.name: Surjectivity via $x=as+br$
nodes.statement: It remains to check it is surjective. Write $1=a+b$ for $a \in \mathfrak{a},b \in \mathfrak{b}$, then for any $(r,s) \in R^2$ the element $x=as+br \in R$ is such that $x \equiv r \pmod \mathfrak{a}$ and $x \equiv s \pmod \mathfrak{b}$ which gives us subjectivity.

nodes.name: CRT for several coprime ideals
nodes.statement: By induction one can extend this to the case where we have several pairwise coprime ideals.

nodes.name: Ideals are generated by two elements
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal. Then for any $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$ with $\alpha$ non-zero we can find $\beta \in \mathfrak{a}$ such that $\mathfrak{a}=(\alpha,\beta)$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Dedekind domain and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal.
conclusions: for any $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$ with $\alpha$ non-zero we can find $\beta \in \mathfrak{a}$ such that $\mathfrak{a}=(\alpha,\beta)$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We will find a $\beta$ such that $\mathfrak{a}=\gcd((\alpha),(\beta))=(\alpha)+(\beta)=(\alpha,\beta)$. Let \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_1^{n_1}\mathfrak{p}_2^{n_2}\cdots\mathfrak{p}_r^{n_r}\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i$ distinct prime ideals. Then since $(\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{a}$ we have $(\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}$ for all $i$, in other words $\alpha$ is divisible by the $\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}$. Now, let $\mathfrak{q}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{q}_s$ be any other prime ideals dividing $(\alpha)$ (if any exist). So we have \[(\alpha)=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i} \times \prod_j \mathfrak{q}_j.\] We construct $\beta$ as follows. Take $\beta_i \in \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i} \backslash \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i+1}$ and then use the Chinese remainder theorem \ref{thm: chinese rem theorem} to find $\beta \in R$ such that $\beta \equiv \beta_i \pmod {\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i+1}}$ for $i \in \{1,\dots,r\}$ and $\beta \equiv 1 \pmod {\mathfrak{q}_j}$ for $j \in \{1,\dots,s\}$. Note that we can do this, and the $\mathfrak{p}_i,\mathfrak{q}_j$ are all pairwise distinct so $\mathfrak{q}_j+\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}=(1)$ (as $\mathfrak{q}_j$ is maximal) for all $i,j$ and moreover, $\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}+\mathfrak{p}_j^{n_j}=\gcd(\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i},\mathfrak{p}_j^{n_j})$ which by Definition \ref{definition: ideal gcd and lcm} is just $(1)$. So now, Definition \ref{definition: ideal gcd and lcm} gives us $\gcd((\alpha),(\beta))=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}=\mathfrak{a}$ and therefore $\beta \in \mathfrak{a}$ which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\beta$ by CRT to have exact valuations $n_i$ at the primes of $\mathfrak{a}$ and be a unit at the other primes of $(\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Goal: $\mathfrak{a}=\gcd((\alpha),(\beta))$
nodes.statement: We will find a $\beta$ such that $\mathfrak{a}=\gcd((\alpha),(\beta))=(\alpha)+(\beta)=(\alpha,\beta)$.

nodes.name: Factor $\mathfrak{a}$ and $(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: Let \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_1^{n_1}\mathfrak{p}_2^{n_2}\cdots\mathfrak{p}_r^{n_r}\] with $\mathfrak{p}_i$ distinct prime ideals. Then since $(\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{a}$ we have $(\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}$ for all $i$, in other words $\alpha$ is divisible by the $\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}$. Now, let $\mathfrak{q}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{q}_s$ be any other prime ideals dividing $(\alpha)$ (if any exist). So we have \[(\alpha)=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i} \times \prod_j \mathfrak{q}_j.\]

nodes.name: Construct $\beta$ by the Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.statement: We construct $\beta$ as follows. Take $\beta_i \in \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i} \backslash \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i+1}$ and then use the Chinese remainder theorem \ref{thm: chinese rem theorem} to find $\beta \in R$ such that $\beta \equiv \beta_i \pmod {\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i+1}}$ for $i \in \{1,\dots,r\}$ and $\beta \equiv 1 \pmod {\mathfrak{q}_j}$ for $j \in \{1,\dots,s\}$. Note that we can do this, and the $\mathfrak{p}_i,\mathfrak{q}_j$ are all pairwise distinct so $\mathfrak{q}_j+\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}=(1)$ (as $\mathfrak{q}_j$ is maximal) for all $i,j$ and moreover, $\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}+\mathfrak{p}_j^{n_j}=\gcd(\mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i},\mathfrak{p}_j^{n_j})$ which by Definition \ref{definition: ideal gcd and lcm} is just $(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\beta$ by the Chinese remainder theorem

nodes.name: gcd computation finishes
nodes.statement: So now, Definition \ref{definition: ideal gcd and lcm} gives us $\gcd((\alpha),(\beta))=\prod_i \mathfrak{p}_i^{n_i}=\mathfrak{a}$ and therefore $\beta \in \mathfrak{a}$ which finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Dedekind UFD iff PID
nodes.statement: A Dedekind domain is a UFD if and only if it is a PID.
equivalent_conditions: A Dedekind domain is a UFD
conclusions: A Dedekind domain is a UFD if and only if it is a PID.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a Dedekind domain that is a PID, then by Proposition \ref{prop: background ring theory} it is a UFD. Now, let $R$ be a UFD and assume for contradiction it is not a PID. Then by Theorem \ref{thm: ded dom ideal is prod of prim} there must exist at least one non-principal prime ideal, call it $\mathfrak{p}$. Now, let $S$ be the set of ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{p}$ is principal. By Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} $S$ is non-empty, so we can do the usual trick and find a maximal element, $\mathfrak{m}$. Let $\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{p}=(\alpha)$, we claim $\alpha$ must be irreducible. Assuming this for the moment, if we take $a \in \mathfrak{p} \backslash (\alpha)$ and $b \in \mathfrak{m} \backslash (\alpha)$ (which we can do in the first case as $\mathfrak{p}$ is not principal and in the second by Exercise \ref{ques: if prod is princ, you are princ}) then $ab \in (\alpha)$ but $\alpha \mid ab$ but $\alpha \nmid a$ and $\alpha \nmid b$ which cannot happen in a UFD. So it remains to prove the claim that $\alpha$ is irreducible. For this we note that if $\alpha=\beta\gamma$ then one of $(\beta)$ or $(\gamma)$ would be of the form $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ for some $\mathfrak{b}$ dividing $\mathfrak{m}$, but $\mathfrak{m}$ is maximal so $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{m}$ and therefore one of $\beta,\gamma$ is a unit.
nodes.statement_short: PID implies UFD; conversely a non-principal prime $\mathfrak{p}$ with maximal $\mathfrak{m}$, $\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{p}=(\alpha)$, yields an irreducible non-prime $\alpha$.

nodes.name: PID implies UFD
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a Dedekind domain that is a PID, then by Proposition \ref{prop: background ring theory} it is a UFD.

nodes.name: UFD not PID: a non-principal prime $\mathfrak{p}$
nodes.statement: Now, let $R$ be a UFD and assume for contradiction it is not a PID. Then by Theorem \ref{thm: ded dom ideal is prod of prim} there must exist at least one non-principal prime ideal, call it $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.statement_short: UFD not PID: a non-principal prime $\mathfrak{p}$

nodes.name: Maximal $\mathfrak{m}$ with $\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{p}$ principal
nodes.statement: Now, let $S$ be the set of ideals $\mathfrak{a}$ such that $\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{p}$ is principal. By Theorem \ref{thm: ideals are invertible} $S$ is non-empty, so we can do the usual trick and find a maximal element, $\mathfrak{m}$.

nodes.name: Claim $\alpha$ irreducible; then it is irreducible but not prime
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{m}\mathfrak{p}=(\alpha)$, we claim $\alpha$ must be irreducible. Assuming this for the moment, if we take $a \in \mathfrak{p} \backslash (\alpha)$ and $b \in \mathfrak{m} \backslash (\alpha)$ (which we can do in the first case as $\mathfrak{p}$ is not principal and in the second by Exercise \ref{ques: if prod is princ, you are princ}) then $ab \in (\alpha)$ but $\alpha \mid ab$ but $\alpha \nmid a$ and $\alpha \nmid b$ which cannot happen in a UFD.
nodes.statement_short: Claim $\alpha$ irreducible; then it is irreducible but not prime

nodes.name: Prove $\alpha$ irreducible by maximality of $\mathfrak{m}$
nodes.statement: So it remains to prove the claim that $\alpha$ is irreducible. For this we note that if $\alpha=\beta\gamma$ then one of $(\beta)$ or $(\gamma)$ would be of the form $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ for some $\mathfrak{b}$ dividing $\mathfrak{m}$, but $\mathfrak{m}$ is maximal so $\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{m}$ and therefore one of $\beta,\gamma$ is a unit.

nodes.name: Norm of an ideal
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ an ideal. We define the norm of $\mathfrak{a}$ to be \[N(\mathfrak{a}):=|\mathcal{O}_K / \mathfrak{a}|.\]

nodes.name: Ideal norm is multiplicative
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$, then \[N(\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b})=N(\mathfrak{a})N(\mathfrak{b}).\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ be ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$,
nodes.label: prop: norm of ideal is mult

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: By factoring each of $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ into prime ideals, it suffices to prove that $N(\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b})=N(\mathfrak{p})N(\mathfrak{b})$ where $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal and $\mathfrak{b}$ is any proper ideal. Now, by group theory $\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ is a subgroup of $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ and the quotient is $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{b}$. This means \[|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|=|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{b}||\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|.\] So we need to show $|\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|=|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}|$. Since $\mathfrak{p} \neq \mathcal{O}_K$ and (fractional) ideals form a group we have $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}\neq \mathfrak{b}$ (otherwise we could multiply through by $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ giving a contradiction), so let $x \in \mathfrak{b} \backslash \mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{p}$. Let us consider the map \[\mathcal{O}_K \longrightarrow \mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}\] given by $a \mapsto ax + \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$. The kernel of this map contains $\mathfrak{p}$ and the map is non-zero by our choice of $x$, so the kernel is an ideal containing $\mathfrak{p}$. But $\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal, so the kernel must be $\mathfrak{p}$. Therefore we have an injective map \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}.\] Now, to see that this map is also surjective we just note that by unique factorization, there cannot be any ideals strictly between $\mathfrak{b}$ and $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$. Since otherwise, we would have $\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{c} \subset \mathfrak{b}$ which means $\mathfrak{b} \mid \mathfrak{c}$ and $\mathfrak{b} \mid \mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{p}$ so by uniqueness of factorization we would have either $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$ or $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{p} \mathfrak{b}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{b}=(x)+\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ giving surjectivity.

nodes.name: Reduce to a prime times an ideal
nodes.statement: By factoring each of $\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}$ into prime ideals, it suffices to prove that $N(\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b})=N(\mathfrak{p})N(\mathfrak{b})$ where $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal and $\mathfrak{b}$ is any proper ideal.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a prime times an ideal

nodes.name: Index computation; need $|\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|=|\mat
nodes.statement: Now, by group theory $\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ is a subgroup of $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ and the quotient is $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{b}$. This means \[|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|=|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{b}||\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|.\] So we need to show $|\mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}|=|\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}|$.

nodes.name: Injective map $a\mapsto ax$
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{p} \neq \mathcal{O}_K$ and (fractional) ideals form a group we have $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}\neq \mathfrak{b}$ (otherwise we could multiply through by $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ giving a contradiction), so let $x \in \mathfrak{b} \backslash \mathfrak{b}\mathfrak{p}$. Let us consider the map \[\mathcal{O}_K \longrightarrow \mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}\] given by $a \mapsto ax + \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$. The kernel of this map contains $\mathfrak{p}$ and the map is non-zero by our choice of $x$, so the kernel is an ideal containing $\mathfrak{p}$. But $\mathfrak{p}$ is maximal, so the kernel must be $\mathfrak{p}$. Therefore we have an injective map \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p} \longrightarrow \mathfrak{b}/\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}.\]

nodes.name: No ideals strictly between
nodes.statement: Now, to see that this map is also surjective we just note that by unique factorization, there cannot be any ideals strictly between $\mathfrak{b}$ and $\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$. Since otherwise, we would have $\mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{c} \subset \mathfrak{b}$ which means $\mathfrak{b} \mid \mathfrak{c}$ and $\mathfrak{b} \mid \mathfrak{b} \mathfrak{p}$ so by uniqueness of factorization we would have either $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{b}$ or $\mathfrak{c}=\mathfrak{p} \mathfrak{b}$.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Therefore $\mathfrak{b}=(x)+\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ giving surjectivity.

nodes.name: Nested ideals with equal norm are equal
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ non-zero ideals. Then $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}$ if and only if $N(\mathfrak{a})=N(\mathfrak{b})$
assumptions: $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ non-zero ideals
nodes.label: lem: containment of ideals equal if norm equal

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Clearly, if $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}$ they have the same norm. So lets check the other direction. First note that since $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$, the tower law (which works for groups) gives us that $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{a}]=[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{b}][\mathfrak{b}:\mathfrak{a}]$. But $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{a}]=N(\mathfrak{a})=N(\mathfrak{b})=[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{b}]$ therefore $[\mathfrak{b}:\mathfrak{a}]=1$ giving the result.

nodes.name: Trivial direction; check the converse
nodes.statement: Clearly, if $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}$ they have the same norm. So lets check the other direction.

nodes.name: Index multiplicativity forces $[\mathfrak{b}:\mathfrak{a}]=1$
nodes.statement: First note that since $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$, the tower law (which works for groups) gives us that $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{a}]=[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{b}][\mathfrak{b}:\mathfrak{a}]$. But $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{a}]=N(\mathfrak{a})=N(\mathfrak{b})=[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathfrak{b}]$ therefore $[\mathfrak{b}:\mathfrak{a}]=1$ giving the result.

nodes.name: Prime norm implies prime; prime ideals have prime power norm
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ an ideal. If $N(\mathfrak{a})$ is a prime, then $\mathfrak{a}$ is a prime ideal. Conversely, if $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal, then $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^f$ for some prime number $p$ and $f \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$.

assumptions: If $N(\mathfrak{a})$ is a prime
if $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal
If $N(\mathfrak{a})$ is a prime
if $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is not prime then $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ with $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal and $\mathfrak{b} \neq (1)$. Then by Proposition \ref{prop: norm of ideal is mult} we have \[N(\mathfrak{a})=N(\mathfrak{p})N(\mathfrak{b})\] which means $N(\mathfrak{a})$ could not have been prime, which is a contradiction. For the converse we note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime it is therefore maximal. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ is a field, which we know is finite. Moreover, we know every finite field has size $p^f$ for some prime $p$ and natural number $f$, which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity of the norm; the residue field is a finite field.

nodes.name: Non-prime ideal has composite norm
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is not prime then $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{b}$ with $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal and $\mathfrak{b} \neq (1)$. Then by Proposition \ref{prop: norm of ideal is mult} we have \[N(\mathfrak{a})=N(\mathfrak{p})N(\mathfrak{b})\] which means $N(\mathfrak{a})$ could not have been prime, which is a contradiction.

nodes.name: Residue field is finite of size $p^f$
nodes.statement: For the converse we note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime it is therefore maximal. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}$ is a field, which we know is finite. Moreover, we know every finite field has size $p^f$ for some prime $p$ and natural number $f$, which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Residue field is finite of size $p^f$

nodes.name: Ideal norm of a principal ideal
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field. Let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K \backslash 0$ and let $(\alpha)$ denote the ideal generated by $\alpha$. Then \[|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|=|\mathcal{O}_K / (\alpha)|.\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field. Let $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K \backslash 0$ and let $(\alpha)$ denote the ideal generated by $\alpha$.
nodes.label: prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be an integral basis of $\mathcal{O}_K$, then clearly $\alpha e_1,\dots,\alpha e_n$ is an integral basis of $(\alpha)$. On the other hand, since $(\alpha) \subset \mathcal{O}_K \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$ we can make sure to choose the $e_i$ such that there exist $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $m_1e_1,\dots,m_ne_n$ is an integral basis of $(\alpha)$. Alternatively, this follows from the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups. Then \[\mathcal{O}_K/(\alpha) \cong \mathbb{Z}/m_1\mathbb{Z} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}/m_n\mathbb{Z}\] and therefore $N((\alpha))=\prod_i |m_i|$. Next we need to relate this number to $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ in some way. For this, let us compare the three bases for $K$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that we have written down: $\{e_1,\dots,\epsilon_n\}$, $\{m_1e_1,\dots,m_ne_n\}$ and $\{\alpha e_1,\dots,\alpha e_n\}$. Now, lets see look at the diagram summarising the associated change of basis matrices. \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} K \arrow[rr, "e_i \mapsto \alpha e_i"] \arrow[dd,"e_i \mapsto e_i",swap] && K \\ \\ K \arrow[rr, "e_i \mapsto m_ie_i",swap] && K \arrow[uu, "m_ie_i \mapsto \alpha e_i",swap] \end{tikzcd} \end{center} The top arrow corresponds to the action of $A_\alpha$. The arrow on the left corresponds to the identity matrix $I$. The arrow along the bottom corresponds to a change of basis matrix with is diagonal which diagonal entries $m_i$, lets call it $D$. Lastly, whatever the matrix corresponding to the arrow going upwards on the right is, it represents a change of basis matrix between two integral bases for $(\alpha)$, therefore similarly to what we have seen before, it must correspond to an invertible matrix with integer coefficients, which we will denote by $N$. Note that this also means, $\det(N)=\pm 1$. Now, from the diagram it is clear that going along the top of the diagram is the same as first going down, then right and then up. This means this is a commutative diagram and therefore we have $A_\alpha=NDI$ therefore \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\det(A_\alpha)=\det(N)\det(D)\det(I)=\pm \det(D)=\prod_i m_i.\] Taking absolute values now gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compare an integral basis, a Smith-form basis of $(\alpha)$ and its image under $A_\alpha$; determinants give $\prod m_i$.

nodes.name: Adapted bases: $N((\alpha))=\prod|m_i|$
nodes.statement: Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be an integral basis of $\mathcal{O}_K$, then clearly $\alpha e_1,\dots,\alpha e_n$ is an integral basis of $(\alpha)$. On the other hand, since $(\alpha) \subset \mathcal{O}_K \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$ we can make sure to choose the $e_i$ such that there exist $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $m_1e_1,\dots,m_ne_n$ is an integral basis of $(\alpha)$. Alternatively, this follows from the structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups. Then \[\mathcal{O}_K/(\alpha) \cong \mathbb{Z}/m_1\mathbb{Z} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}/m_n\mathbb{Z}\] and therefore $N((\alpha))=\prod_i |m_i|$.

nodes.name: Compare three bases
nodes.statement: Next we need to relate this number to $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ in some way. For this, let us compare the three bases for $K$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that we have written down: $\{e_1,\dots,\epsilon_n\}$, $\{m_1e_1,\dots,m_ne_n\}$ and $\{\alpha e_1,\dots,\alpha e_n\}$.

nodes.name: Diagram of change-of-basis maps
nodes.statement: Now, lets see look at the diagram summarising the associated change of basis matrices. \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} K \arrow[rr, "e_i \mapsto \alpha e_i"] \arrow[dd,"e_i \mapsto e_i",swap] && K \\ \\ K \arrow[rr, "e_i \mapsto m_ie_i",swap] && K \arrow[uu, "m_ie_i \mapsto \alpha e_i",swap] \end{tikzcd} \end{center}

nodes.name: Identify the matrices $A_\alpha$, $I$, $D$, $N$
nodes.statement: The top arrow corresponds to the action of $A_\alpha$. The arrow on the left corresponds to the identity matrix $I$. The arrow along the bottom corresponds to a change of basis matrix with is diagonal which diagonal entries $m_i$, lets call it $D$. Lastly, whatever the matrix corresponding to the arrow going upwards on the right is, it represents a change of basis matrix between two integral bases for $(\alpha)$, therefore similarly to what we have seen before, it must correspond to an invertible matrix with integer coefficients, which we will denote by $N$. Note that this also means, $\det(N)=\pm 1$.

nodes.name: Take determinants
nodes.statement: Now, from the diagram it is clear that going along the top of the diagram is the same as first going down, then right and then up. This means this is a commutative diagram and therefore we have $A_\alpha=NDI$ therefore \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\det(A_\alpha)=\det(N)\det(D)\det(I)=\pm \det(D)=\prod_i m_i.\] Taking absolute values now gives the result.

nodes.name: (lambda_p) is a prime ideal
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a odd prime, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $\lambda_p=1-\zeta_p$. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Then from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: ring of ints of cyclo} we know $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\lambda_p)=p$ and therefore $N((\lambda_p))=p$ which by the above means, $(\lambda_p)$ must be a prime ideal.

nodes.name: Principal iff norms match
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field, $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ an ideal and $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$. Then $\mathfrak{a}=(\alpha)$ if and only if $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|=N(\mathfrak{a})$.
assumptions: $K$ be a number field, $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ an ideal and $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}$ we have $(\alpha) \subset \mathfrak{a}$. Then by Lemma \ref{lem: containment of ideals equal if norm equal} and Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm} gives the result.

nodes.name: An ideal contains its norm
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ a non-zero ideal. Let $a=N(\mathfrak{a})$. Then $a \in \mathfrak{a}$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ a non-zero ideal. Let $a=N(\mathfrak{a})$.
nodes.label: lem: ideal contains its norm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Recall that by Lagrange's Theorem, every element in $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$ has order at most $a$. Therefore, if we look at the element $1+\mathfrak{a} \in \mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{a}$ we have $a\cdot (1+\mathfrak{a})=0 +\mathfrak{a}$ therefore $a \in \mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Comparison with earlier proof
nodes.statement: We've seen something similar in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop: quot of ideal is finite}.

nodes.name: Finitely many ideals of given norm
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field. Then there are only finitely many ideals with a given norm.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field.
conclusions: there are only finitely many ideals with a given norm.
nodes.label: cor: fin many ideals of given norm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal with $N(\mathfrak{a})=a$ then by Lemma \ref{lem: ideal contains its norm} we have $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ which means $\mathfrak{a} \mid (a)$. But by uniqueness of factorization, $a$ only has finitely many factors, which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Such ideals divide $(a)$, which has finitely many divisors.

nodes.name: Prime lying over
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$. If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$ then we say $\mathfrak{P}$ lies over $\mathfrak{p}$ (or equivalently $\mathfrak{p}$ lies under $\mathfrak{P}$), if $\mathfrak{P} \mid \mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$. Here $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ denotes the ideal generated by $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$.

nodes.name: Characterizations of lying over
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$. If $\mathfrak{P}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $K$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $F$ then the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item $\mathfrak{P} \mid \mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ \item $\mathfrak{P} \supset \mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ \item $\mathfrak{P} \supset \mathfrak{p}$ \item $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$ \item $\mathfrak{P} \cap F=\mathfrak{p}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$
$\mathfrak{P}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $K$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a non-zero prime ideal in $F$
nodes.label: prop: prime above

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor: ideal div} gives that $(1)$ and $(2)$ are equivalent. Since $\mathfrak{P}$ is an ideal, if it contains $\mathfrak{p}$ it contains $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$, therefore $(2)$ and $(3)$ are equivalent. Since $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ it follows that $(4)$ and $(5)$ are equivalent. So it remains to prove $(3)$ and $(4)$ are equivalent. It obvious that $(4) \implies (3)$ so we just need the reverse. Note that $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F$ contains $\mathfrak{p}$ and is moreover an ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$. But now, since every prime ideal in a Dedekind domain is maximal, $\mathfrak{p}$ is also maximal and therefore we must have $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$ or $ \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathcal{O}_F$. But if $ \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathcal{O}_F$ then $1 \in \mathfrak{P}$ meaning $\mathfrak{P}=\mathcal{O}_K$ which contradicts it being a prime ideal.
nodes.statement_short: Chain of easy equivalences; (3)$\Rightarrow$(4) by maximality of $\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(2)
nodes.statement: Corollary \ref{cor: ideal div} gives that $(1)$ and $(2)$ are equivalent.

nodes.name: (2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3)
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{P}$ is an ideal, if it contains $\mathfrak{p}$ it contains $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$, therefore $(2)$ and $(3)$ are equivalent.

nodes.name: (4)$\Leftrightarrow$(5)
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ it follows that $(4)$ and $(5)$ are equivalent.

nodes.name: Remains (3)$\Rightarrow$(4)
nodes.statement: So it remains to prove $(3)$ and $(4)$ are equivalent. It obvious that $(4) \implies (3)$ so we just need the reverse.

nodes.name: Maximality of $\mathfrak{p}$
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F$ contains $\mathfrak{p}$ and is moreover an ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$. But now, since every prime ideal in a Dedekind domain is maximal, $\mathfrak{p}$ is also maximal and therefore we must have $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$ or $ \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathcal{O}_F$.

nodes.name: Exclude the whole ring
nodes.statement: But if $ \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathcal{O}_F$ then $1 \in \mathfrak{P}$ meaning $\mathfrak{P}=\mathcal{O}_K$ which contradicts it being a prime ideal.

nodes.name: (2,1+sqrt3) lies over (2)
nodes.statement: If we take $F=\mathbb{Q}$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})$ then $(2,1+\sqrt{3})$ lies above $(2)$. To see this we just note that $(2,1+\sqrt{3}) \cap \mathbb{Z}=(2)$.

nodes.name: Going up: primes lie over unique primes
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$. Then every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ lies over a unique non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$. Conversely, every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$ lies under at least one non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$.
nodes.statement_short: Each nonzero prime of $\mathcal{O}_K$ lies over a unique prime of $\mathcal{O}_F$, and each prime of $\mathcal{O}_F$ lies under some prime of $\mathcal{O}_K$.

conclusions: every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ lies over a unique non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$
every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$ lies under at least one non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$

assumptions: $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$
conclusions: every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ lies over a unique non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$
every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$ lies under at least one non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{P} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$

So we are reduced to checking $1 \not \in \mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K.$ By Lemma \ref{lem: proper ideal mult by frac is still int} we can find $x \in F \backslash \mathcal{O}_F$ such that $x \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$. If $1 \in \mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ then $x \in \mathcal{O}_K$, but then $x$ is in $\mathcal{O}_K \cap F=\mathcal{O}_F$ and this an algebraic integer, contradicting the fact that $x \in F \backslash \mathcal{O}_F$.

nodes.name: Ramification index and inertial degree
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields with rings of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathcal{O}_F$ and let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a non-zero prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$. Then \[\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K= \prod_{i=1}^r \mathfrak{P}_i^{e_i}.\] We call the $e_i$ the \textit{ramification indices} and if needed we will denote them by $e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}$. Now, let $\mathfrak{P}$ lie over $\mathfrak{p}$. Recall that $k_{\mathfrak{P}}:=\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}$ and $k_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\mathcal{O}_F/\mathfrak{p}$ are both finite fields, since $\mathfrak{P},\mathfrak{p}$ are both maximal ideals and by Proposition \ref{prop: quot of ideal is finite} we know the quotient ring is always finite. These are called the \textit{residual fields} attached to $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ respectively. Moreover, $k_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is naturally a subfield of $k_{\mathfrak{P}}$ (convince yourself of this). Therefore, $k_{\mathfrak{P}}$ is a finite extension of $k_{\mathfrak{p}}$ and $[k_{\mathfrak{P}}:k_{\mathfrak{p}}]$ is called the \textit{inertial degree} or \textit{residue degree} of $\mathfrak{P}$ over $\mathfrak{p}$, which will be denoted $f_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $e$ = exponent of $\mathfrak{P}$ in $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$; $f=[k_\mathfrak{P}:k_\mathfrak{p}]$ for the residue fields.
nodes.label: definition: ram index and inert deg

nodes.name: Multiplicativity of e and f in towers
nodes.statement: Let $F \subset K \subset L$ be number fields and $p \subset \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{P}$ be prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_F \subset \mathcal{O}_K \subset \mathcal{O}_L$. Then \[e_{\mathfrak{P}|p}=e_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}e_{\mathfrak{p}|p} \] and \[f_{\mathfrak{P}|p}=f_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}f_{\mathfrak{p}|p} \]
assumptions: Let $F \subset K \subset L$ be number fields and $p \subset \mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{P}$ be prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_F \subset \mathcal{O}_K \subset \mathcal{O}_L$.
nodes.label: prop: tow law for ram rel

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: For the $f$'s this follows easily from the Tower Law \ref{prop: tower law}. For the $e$'s the result is clear.
nodes.statement_short: Tower law for residue fields; clear for $e$.

nodes.name: Fundamental identity sum e_i f_i = n
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=n$ and $p$ a prime number. If $\mathfrak{p}_i$ are the prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$ dividing $p\mathcal{O}_K$, then \[\sum_i e_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}=n\] with notation as in Definition \ref{definition: ram index and inert deg}.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field with $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=n$ and $p$ a prime number. If $\mathfrak{p}_i$ are the prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$ dividing $p\mathcal{O}_K$,
conclusions: \[\sum_i e_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}=n\] with notation as in Definition \ref{definition: ram index and inert deg}.
nodes.label: thm: ram-rel

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Let $e_i:=e_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$ and $f_i:=f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$. By definition we have \[p\mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{p}_1^{e_1}\mathfrak{p}_2^{e_2}\dots\mathfrak{p}_r^{e_r}.\] Now, lets take norms on both sides: By Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm} we have $N(p\mathcal{O}_K)=|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)|=p^n$. So we have \[p^n=\prod_i N(\mathfrak{p}_i)^{e_i}.\] So it remains to show that $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^{f_i}$. For this we note that $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{F}_p:=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}=:k_p$ of degree $[k_{\mathfrak{p}_i}/k_p]=f_i$. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}_i \cong \mathbb{F}_p^{f_i}$ (as a vector space) from which it follows that $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^{f_i}$.

nodes.name: Factor $p\mathcal{O}_K$ and take norms
nodes.statement: Let $e_i:=e_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$ and $f_i:=f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$. By definition we have \[p\mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{p}_1^{e_1}\mathfrak{p}_2^{e_2}\dots\mathfrak{p}_r^{e_r}.\] Now, lets take norms on both sides: By Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm} we have $N(p\mathcal{O}_K)=|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)|=p^n$.

nodes.name: Remains $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^{f_i}$
nodes.statement: So we have \[p^n=\prod_i N(\mathfrak{p}_i)^{e_i}.\] So it remains to show that $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^{f_i}$.

nodes.name: Residue field has $p^{f_i}$ elements
nodes.statement: For this we note that $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{F}_p:=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}=:k_p$ of degree $[k_{\mathfrak{p}_i}/k_p]=f_i$. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{p}_i \cong \mathbb{F}_p^{f_i}$ (as a vector space) from which it follows that $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^{f_i}$.

nodes.name: Fundamental identity for relative extensions
nodes.statement: \sum_i e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}f_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}=[K:F]
nodes.label: eqn: ram rel

nodes.name: Ideal norm in towers
nodes.statement: Let $K,F$ be a number fields with $[K:F]=n$. Let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$ and let $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{a}\mathcal{O}_K$, then \[N(\mathfrak{A})=N(\mathfrak{a})^n\]
assumptions: Let $K,F$ be a number fields with $[K:F]=n$. Let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$ and let $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{a}\mathcal{O}_K$,
nodes.label: prop: ideal norm in tower

nodes.name: Prove relative fundamental identity
nodes.statement: Using Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm in tower} prove \ref{eqn: ram rel}.

nodes.name: Dedekind--Kummer
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be an extension of number fields and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ a primitive element so that $K \cong F(\alpha)$. Let $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_F$ be a prime ideal and $p$ the prime number such that $(p)=\mathfrak{p} \cap \mathbb{Z}$. Assume that $p$ does not divide the index\footnote{Note that here I am thinking of $\mathcal{O}_F[\alpha]$ as a subgroup of $\mathcal{O}_K$ and then $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathcal{O}_F[\alpha]]$ denotes the size of the quotient group $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathcal{O}_F[\alpha]$. } \[[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathcal{O}_F[\alpha]].\] Let $m_{\alpha,F}$ be the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $F$ and let \[\overline{m}_{\alpha,F} \in (\mathcal{O}_F/\mathfrak{p})[x]\] be its reduction modulo $\mathfrak{p}$. Now, write $\overline{m}_{\alpha,F}$ as a product of powers of irreducible polynomials (i.e factorize it) \[\overline{m}_{\alpha,F}(x)=\overline{m}_1(x)^{e_1}\dots \overline{m}_r(x)^{e_r}.\] Next, let $m_i \in \mathcal{O}_F[x]$ be a polynomial whose reduction modulo $\mathfrak{p}$ is $\overline{m}_i$ and let \[\mathfrak{P}_i=(\mathfrak{p},m_i(\alpha))=\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K+(m_i(\alpha)).\] Then: \begin{enumerate} \item The ideals $\mathfrak{P}_i$ are independent of choice of $m_i$. (This is by construction) \item The $\mathfrak{P}_i$ are distinct prime ideals and they are precisely the prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}_K$ lying over $\mathfrak{p}$. Therefore \[\mathfrak{p} \mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{P}_1^{e_1}\dots\mathfrak{P}_r^{e_r}\] \item $f_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}=\deg(\overline{m}_i)$ and $e_i=e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: If $p\nmid[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathcal{O}_F[\alpha]]$, primes over $\mathfrak{p}$ are $(\mathfrak{p},m_i(\alpha))$ for the irreducible factors $\overline{m}_i^{e_i}$ of $m_{\alpha,F}$ mod $\mathfrak{p}$, with $f=\deg\overline{m}_i$.
assumptions: $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ a primitive element so that $K \cong F(\alpha)$
Assume that $p$ does not divide the index
conclusions: The $\mathfrak{P}_i$ are distinct prime ideals and they are precisely the prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}_K$ lying over $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.label: thm: ded-kum

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
The result will follow from the following three claims:  egin{enumerate}[(A)] \item[A] Let $f_i=\deg(\overline{m}_i)$. For each $i$, either $\mathfrak{P}_i=\mathcal{O}_K$ or $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}_i$ is a field of size $|\mathcal{O}_F/\mathfrak{p}|^{f_i}$. \item[B] $\mathfrak{P}_i+\mathfrak{P}_j=\mathcal{O}_K$ whenever $i 
eq j$. \item [C] $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ divides $\mathfrak{P}_1^{e_1}\dots\mathfrak{P}_r^{e_r}$. \end{enumerate} From this we get the result as follows: By relabelling the $\mathfrak{P}_i$ we can assume that $\mathfrak{P}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{P}_s 
eq \mathcal{O}_K$ and $\mathfrak{P}_{s+1},\dots,\mathfrak{P}_r=\mathcal{O}_K$. Now, from ((1)) it follows that $\mathfrak{P}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{P}_s$ are all prime ideals (since quotienting out by them gives a field). Moreover, by construction they contain $\mathfrak{p}$, so lie above $\mathfrak{p}$ and $f_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}=f_i$ (to see this just look at how the residue degrees are defined). Next ((2)) tells us that $\mathfrak{P}_1,\dots,\mathfrak{P}_s$ are all distinct and ((3)) becomes \[\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K \mid \mathfrak{P}_1^{e_1}\dots\mathfrak{P}_s^{e_s}.\] From this it follows that \[\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K = \mathfrak{P}_1^{d_1}\dots\mathfrak{P}_s^{d_s}\] with $d_i \leq e_i$. Now, using ef{eqn: ram rel} we have \[[K:F]=\sum_{i=1}^s d_if_i\] but on the other hand \[\deg(m_{\alpha,F})=[K:F]=\sum_{i=1}^r e_if_i.\] So comparing these gives $r=s$, $d_i=e_i$ for all $i$. So lets prove these three claims.  egin{proof}[Proof of (1)] Note that each $\overline{m}_i$ is an irreducible polynomial in $(\mathcal{O}_F/\mathfrak{p})[x]$. So if we let $E:=\mathcal{O}_F/\mathfrak{p}$ (which is a field), then $M_i:=E[x]/\overline{m}_i$ is again a field. We have a map \[\mathcal{O}_F[x] \longrightarrow M_i\] given by first reducing modulo $\mathfrak{p}$ and then modulo $\overline{m}_i$. This map is clearly surjective and the kernel is given by the ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F[x]$ generated by $\mathfrak{p}$ and $m_i$. So we have an isomorphism \[\mathcal{O}_F[x]/(\mathfrak{p},m_i) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} M_i.\] Alongside this, note that we have a ring homomorphism \[\phi:\mathcal{O}_F[x] \longrightarrow \mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}_i\] given by evaluation at $\alpha$ (i.e $x \mapsto \alpha$) and reducing modulo $\mathfrak{P}_i$. By definition of $\mathfrak{P}_i$ its clear that $(\mathfrak{p},m_i)$ is in the kernel. nodes.name: Ramified, inert and split primes
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $p$ a prime number. We say \begin{enumerate} \item $p$ is \textit{ramified} in $K$, if there exists a $\mathfrak{p}|p$ such that $e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}>1$. Otherwise we say $p$ is \textit{unramified}. \item $p$ is \textit{totally ramified} if there is a $\mathfrak{p}|p$ such that $e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$. \item $p$ is \textit{inert} if $p$ is unramified and there exists a unique prime $\mathfrak{p}$ lying above $p$ (which will have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$). \item $p$ is \textit{ split} if it is unramified and for some $\mathfrak{p}|p$ we have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=1$. If it is unramified and for all $\mathfrak{p}|p$ we we have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=1$, we say $p$ is \textit{totally split}. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Splitting of 2, 3, 11 in Z[sqrt-5]
