Therefore $(2)$ is totally ramified in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$. Similarly, if we look at the ideal $(3)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, we find that \[(3)=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})(3,1-\sqrt{-5})\] where again each idea on the right is now prime. So $(3)$ totally splits in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$. Lastly, if we look at $(11)$ we will see that this remains prime in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ and is therefore inert.
also_stated_at: In $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, the ideal $(2)$ is no longer prime, since we will see that \[(2)=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})^2\] where now $(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ is a prime ideal in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$. (You actually have enough to check this. You can compute its norm and see that it has norm $2$) Similarly, if we look at the ideal $(3)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, we find that \[(3)=(3,1+\sqrt{-5})(3,1-\sqrt{-5})\] where again each idea on the right is now prime.

nodes.name: Splitting of primes in Q(sqrt6) and factoring (12+7sqrt6)
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{6})$ (so here $\alpha=\sqrt{6}$). From Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} we have $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{6}]$ and therefore $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]=1$ so Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} works for any prime number. Now, note that $m_\alpha=x^2-6$. Lets use this to find how the ideal $2\mathcal{O}_K$ factorizes in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{6}]$. From now on I will just denote $p\mathcal{O}_K$ by $(p)$. First step is to reduce $m_\alpha$ modulo $2$. Which gives $\overline{m}_\alpha(x)=x^2=\overline{m}_1(x)^2$ (if you cant see why we only have one $\overline{m}_i$ on the right hand side, just look back at the theorem and note that the $\overline{m}_i$ are distinct by construction). Next, we need to find some $m_1(x)$ whose reduction modulo $(2)$ agrees with $\overline{m}_1(x)$. For this lets just be lazy and take $m_1(x)=x$ (this might be a good point to comeback to and try and convince yourself the the choice of $m_1(x)$ wont make a difference to then end result, i.e. see what happens if we take $m_1(x)=x+2$). The theorem then says that \[(2)=\mathfrak{p}_2^2:=(2,\sqrt{6})^2.\] This means $(2)$ ramifies in $\mathcal{O}_K$. Ok lets do some more examples. To speed things up here is a table of values of $m_\alpha(x)$ for some small $x$ which is useful for figuring out how $m_\alpha$ factorizes modulo $p$. \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{ | c | c | } \hline $x$ & $m_\alpha(x)=x^2-6$ \\ \hline $0$ & $-6$ \\ \hline $\pm 1$ & $-5$ \\ \hline $\pm 2$ & $-2$ \\ \hline $\pm 3$ & $3$ \\ \hline $\pm 4$ & $10$ \\ \hline $\pm 5$ & $19$ \\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center} From this table we see that: \begin{align*} &m_\alpha(x)=x^2 \pmod 3\\ &m_\alpha(x)=(x-1)(x+1) \pmod 5\\ &m_\alpha(x)=(x^2-6) \pmod 7\\ &m_\alpha(x)=(x^2-6) \pmod {11}\\ \end{align*} From this it follows that: \begin{align*} &(3)=\mathfrak{p}_3^2:=(3,\sqrt{6})^2 \\ &(5)=\mathfrak{p}_5\mathfrak{p}_5':=(5,\sqrt{6}-1)(5,\sqrt{6}+1)\\ &(7)=\mathfrak{p}_7:=(7)\\ &(11)=\mathfrak{p}_{11}:= (11)\\ \end{align*} So we see that $(3)$ ramified in $\mathcal{O}_K$, $(5)$ splits and $(7),(11)$ are inert in $\mathcal{O}_K$. BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE (insert relevant meme): The theorem tells us the norm of the ideals $\mathfrak{p}$. Specifically, the theorem says that $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=\deg(\overline{m}_i)$ and by Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} we saw $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^{f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}}$. So, in this case we get \begin{align*} &N(\mathfrak{p}_2)=2 \\ &N(\mathfrak{p}_3)=3 \\ &N(\mathfrak{p}_5)=5^1 \text{ and } N(\mathfrak{p}_5')=5^1 \\ &N(\mathfrak{p}_7)=7^2 \\ &N(\mathfrak{p}_{11})=11^2 \\ \end{align*} We can also use this factorize other ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$. \begin{enumerate} \item Say $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal, then we can first calculate $N(\mathfrak{a})$ (which if $\mathfrak{a}$ is principal we know how to do, but in general this might be hard) and factorize it. \item For each prime number $p$ appearing, we then factor $(p)$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ as we did above. \item Note that Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm} tells us that there are only finitely many prime ideals of norm $p$, we can find them all by looking at the factorization of $(p)$. \item Next we use Proposition \ref{cor: ideal div}, tells us that $\mathfrak{p} | \mathfrak{a}$ if and only if the generators of $\mathfrak{p}$ are in $\mathfrak{a}$. \end{enumerate} Lets do this for $\mathfrak{a}=(12+7\sqrt{6})$. To find the norm of this ideal we use Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm} this gives \[N(\mathfrak{a})=|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(12+7\sqrt{6})|=|12^2-6\cdot7^2|=150=2\cdot 3 \cdot 5^2\] From the above calculation we see that $\mathfrak{p}_2$ is the only prime ideal of norm $2$ and $\mathfrak{p}_3$ is the only prime ideal of norm $3$ and that we have two ideals of norm $5$. This immediately gives us that there are only 3 ideals of norm $150$ and they are \[\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5^2 \qquad \mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5'^2 \qquad \mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5\mathfrak{p}_5'\] So we need to check with one of these is $\mathfrak{a}$. First we see that since $\mathfrak{p}_5\mathfrak{p}_5'=(5)$ and $12+7\sqrt{6}$ is not a multiple of $5$, it follows it can't be the one with a $\mathfrak{p}_5\mathfrak{p}_5'$ term. Now, note that $12+7\sqrt{6}=5+7(1+\sqrt{6})$ therefore its contained in $\mathfrak{p}_5'$ and therefore \[\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5'^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: Dedekind--Kummer in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt6]$: 2, 3 ramify, 5 splits, 7, 11 inert; then $(12+7\sqrt6)=\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5'^2$.

nodes.name: Factoring an ideal via its norm
nodes.statement: We can also use this factorize other ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$. \begin{enumerate} \item Say $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal, then we can first calculate $N(\mathfrak{a})$ (which if $\mathfrak{a}$ is principal we know how to do, but in general this might be hard) and factorize it. \item For each prime number $p$ appearing, we then factor $(p)$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ as we did above. \item Note that Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm} tells us that there are only finitely many prime ideals of norm $p$, we can find them all by looking at the factorization of $(p)$. \item Next we use Proposition \ref{cor: ideal div}, tells us that $\mathfrak{p} | \mathfrak{a}$ if and only if the generators of $\mathfrak{p}$ are in $\mathfrak{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $N(\mathfrak{a})$, factor each $(p)$, list the prime ideals of each norm, test which divide $\mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Compute and factor $N(\mathfrak{a})$
nodes.statement: Say $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal, then we can first calculate $N(\mathfrak{a})$ (which if $\mathfrak{a}$ is principal we know how to do, but in general this might be hard) and factorize it.

nodes.name: Factor each $(p)$
nodes.statement: For each prime number $p$ appearing, we then factor $(p)$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ as we did above.

nodes.name: List the finitely many primes of norm $p$
nodes.statement: Note that Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm} tells us that there are only finitely many prime ideals of norm $p$, we can find them all by looking at the factorization of $(p)$.
nodes.statement_short: List the finitely many primes of norm $p$

nodes.name: Test divisibility via generators
nodes.statement: Next we use Proposition \ref{cor: ideal div}, tells us that $\mathfrak{p} | \mathfrak{a}$ if and only if the generators of $\mathfrak{p}$ are in $\mathfrak{a}$.

nodes.name: Splitting of primes in a cubic field x^3+10x+1
nodes.statement: Lets do a cubic. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ where $\alpha$ is a root of $m_\alpha(x)=x^3+10x+1$. This is irreducible since it is irreducible in $\mathbb{F}_{13}$ (just check it doesnt have a root). By Corollary \ref{cor: disc of cubic field} we have that \[\Delta(\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2\})=-4027\] which is a prime number, in particular it is square-free, so this is an integral basis by Corollary \ref{cor: square free implies int basis}. So $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$. So we can freely apply Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum}. Lets see how some prime split in $K$: We have \[\overline{m}_\alpha(x)=(x+1)(x^2+x+1) \mod 2,\] therefore \[(2)=\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_2'=(2,\alpha+1)(2,\alpha^2+\alpha+1).\] Thus $(2)$ is unramified, and the residue degrees are $f_{\mathfrak{p}_2|2}=1$ and $f_{\mathfrak{p}_2'|2}=2$. Lets look at $(29)$. Here we see that \[\overline{m}_\alpha(x)=(x+5)(x-3)(x-2) \mod 29\] meaning \[(29)=\mathfrak{p}_{29}\mathfrak{p}_{29}'\mathfrak{p}_{29}''=(29,\alpha+5)(29,\alpha-3)(29,\alpha-2).\] Thus $(29)$ is also unramified and in particular it is totally split. So the residue degrees are all $1$. Lastly, lets look at $(4027)$. Here we see \[\overline{m}_\alpha(x)=(x+2215)^2(x+3624) \mod 4027\] therefore \[(4027)=\mathfrak{p}_{4027}^2\mathfrak{p}_{4027}'=(4027,\alpha+2215)^2(4027,\alpha+3624).\] Thus $(4027)$ is ramified. $e_{\mathfrak{p}_{4027}|4027}=2$, $e_{\mathfrak{p}_{4027}'|4027}=1$ and the residue degrees are all $1$.

nodes.name: Eisenstein primes are totally ramified
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ a primitive element with $m_\alpha$ Eisenstein at $p$. Then we have \[(p)=\mathfrak{p}^{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}\] with $\mathfrak{p}=(p,\alpha)$.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ a primitive element with $m_\alpha$ Eisenstein at $p$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $\alpha$ is Eisenstein at $p$ then $\frac{\mathcal{O}_K}{\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]}$ has no element of order $p$ by Lemma \ref{lem: eis crit and alg ints} and therefore the index $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]]$ is coprime to $p$. So we can apply Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} which, since $m_\alpha$ is Eisenstein at $p$, gives $\overline{m}_\alpha(x)=x^{[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$, from which the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Eisenstein lemma gives $p\nmid$ index; Dedekind--Kummer with $\overline{m}_\alpha=x^n$.

nodes.name: Possible decompositions in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: (p) = \begin{cases} \mathfrak{p}^2, & f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=1 \\ \mathfrak{p}, & f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=2 \\ \mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{p}', & f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f_{\mathfrak{p}'|p}=1 \end{cases}

nodes.name: Splitting of primes in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a square-free integer, $K:=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{n})$ and $p$ a prime number. \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] If $p\mid n$ then $(p)=(p,\sqrt{n})^2$. \item[(2)] If $n$ is odd then \[ (2)= \begin{cases} (2,1+\sqrt{n})^2, & \text{if } n \equiv 3 \pmod 4 \hspace{0.5cm} (3.3) \\ \left(2,\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}\right)\left(2,\frac{1-\sqrt{n}}{2}\right) & \text{if } n \equiv 1 \pmod 8 \hspace{0.5cm} (3.4)\\ (2) &\text{if } n \equiv 5 \pmod 8 \hspace{0.5cm} (3.5) \end{cases} \] \item[(3)] If $p$ is odd and $p \nmid n$, then \[(p)=\begin{cases} (p,a+\sqrt{n}) (p,a-\sqrt{n}) & \text{if } n \equiv a^2 \pmod p \hspace{0.5cm} (3.6)\\ (p) &\text{if } \left( \frac{n}{p}\right)=-1 \end{cases}\] \end{enumerate} Moreover, in (3.4) and (3.6) the ideals appearing are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: Ramified for $p\mid n$; behaviour of 2 by $n$ mod 8; odd $p\nmid n$ split or inert by the Legendre symbol $(n/p)$.

assumptions: If $p\mid n$
If $n$ is odd
If $p$ is odd and $p \nmid n$

conclusions: Moreover, in (3.4) and (3.6) the ideals appearing are distinct.

assumptions: $n$ be a square-free integer, $K:=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{n})$ and $p$ a prime number.
If $p\mid n$
If $n$ is odd
If $p$ is odd and $p \nmid n$
conclusions: Moreover, in (3.4) and (3.6) the ideals appearing are distinct.
nodes.label: thm: splitting in quad ext

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We will defer the proof that the ideals in (3.4) and (3.6) are distinct to Corollary \ref{cor: ids are disc}. For (1), note that $(p,\sqrt{n})^2=(p^2,p\sqrt{n},n)$, which if $p \mid n$ is contained in $(p)$. Conversely, $(p^2,p\sqrt{n},n)$ contains the GCD of $p^2$ and $n$, which is $p$, so we get $(p) \subset (p,\sqrt{n})^2$, therefore we get the equality we are after. We will split the rest of proof into two cases, which together give the result. The first is if $n \equiv 2,3 \pmod 4$ and the second if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. From Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} we know that if $n \equiv 2,3 \pmod 4$ then $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{n}]$. In this case Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} (using $\alpha=\sqrt{n}$ and $m_\alpha=x^2-n$) gives (3) and (3.3) (which is the only one that applies in this case). Now, we look at the case $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. In this case, Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} tells us that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}]$. Note that this means the index $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{n}]]=2$ but $p$ is odd, so it doesn't divide this index. So Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} gives (3). So, we are left with (3.4) and (3.5) of (2). Here we cannot apply Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum}. So lets assume $n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, then \[ \left (2,\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}\right )\left (2,\frac{1-\sqrt{n}}{2}\right )=\left(4,1-\sqrt{n},1+\sqrt{n},\frac{1-n}{4}\right).\] Now, since each of these generators is divisible by $2$, we get that \[\left(2,\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}\right)\left(2,\frac{1-\sqrt{n}}{2}\right) \subset (2).\] Conversely, $\left(4,1-\sqrt{n},1+\sqrt{n},\frac{1-n}{4}\right)$ contains the $\gcd(4,1-\sqrt{n})=2$ which gives the reverse inclusion. Finally, lets assume $n \equiv 5 \pmod 8$. In this case lets consider $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} its enough to show that $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ is a field not isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (since this means the residue degree is $2$ and therefore, since we are in a quadratic field, it must be inert). To show they are not isomorphic, consider \[m_\alpha(x)=x^2-x+\frac{1-n}{4}.\] By construction, this has a root in $\mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore has a root in $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ (just reduce your root modulo $2$). On the other hand, since $n \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ we have $m_\alpha(x)=x^2+x+1 \pmod 2$ which by Exercise \ref{ques: irr pol mod 2} we know is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and therefore has no root in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. So $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ is an extension of $\mathbb{F}_2$ by a root of $x^2+x+1$, so its a field, which also goes by the name $\mathbb{F}_4$.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $n$ mod 4 via Dedekind--Kummer; for $p=2$, $n\equiv1 \bmod 4$ compute the product directly or show $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)\cong\mathbb{F}_4$.

nodes.name: Distinctness deferred to a later corollary
nodes.statement: We will defer the proof that the ideals in (3.4) and (3.6) are distinct to Corollary \ref{cor: ids are disc}.
nodes.statement_short: Distinctness deferred to a later corollary

nodes.name: Case $p\mid n$: compute $(p,\sqrt n)^2$
nodes.statement: For (1), note that $(p,\sqrt{n})^2=(p^2,p\sqrt{n},n)$, which if $p \mid n$ is contained in $(p)$. Conversely, $(p^2,p\sqrt{n},n)$ contains the GCD of $p^2$ and $n$, which is $p$, so we get $(p) \subset (p,\sqrt{n})^2$, therefore we get the equality we are after.

nodes.name: Split by $n$ mod 4
nodes.statement: We will split the rest of proof into two cases, which together give the result. The first is if $n \equiv 2,3 \pmod 4$ and the second if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

nodes.name: $n\equiv2,3$: Dedekind--Kummer with $x^2-n$
nodes.statement: From Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} we know that if $n \equiv 2,3 \pmod 4$ then $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{n}]$. In this case Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} (using $\alpha=\sqrt{n}$ and $m_\alpha=x^2-n$) gives (3) and (3.3) (which is the only one that applies in this case).

nodes.name: $n\equiv1$, odd $p$: index 2 is prime to $p$
nodes.statement: Now, we look at the case $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. In this case, Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} tells us that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}]$. Note that this means the index $[\mathcal{O}_K:\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{n}]]=2$ but $p$ is odd, so it doesn't divide this index. So Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} gives (3).

nodes.name: $n\equiv1 \bmod 8$: product of the two ideals is $(2)$
nodes.statement: So, we are left with (3.4) and (3.5) of (2). Here we cannot apply Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum}. So lets assume $n \equiv 1 \pmod 8$, then \[ \left (2,\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}\right )\left (2,\frac{1-\sqrt{n}}{2}\right )=\left(4,1-\sqrt{n},1+\sqrt{n},\frac{1-n}{4}\right).\] Now, since each of these generators is divisible by $2$, we get that \[\left(2,\frac{1+\sqrt{n}}{2}\right)\left(2,\frac{1-\sqrt{n}}{2}\right) \subset (2).\] Conversely, $\left(4,1-\sqrt{n},1+\sqrt{n},\frac{1-n}{4}\right)$ contains the $\gcd(4,1-\sqrt{n})=2$ which gives the reverse inclusion.
nodes.statement_short: $n\equiv1 \bmod 8$: product of the two ideals is $(2)$

nodes.name: $n\equiv5 \bmod 8$: $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)\cong\mathbb{F}_4$, so 2 is iner
nodes.statement: Finally, lets assume $n \equiv 5 \pmod 8$. In this case lets consider $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} its enough to show that $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ is a field not isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (since this means the residue degree is $2$ and therefore, since we are in a quadratic field, it must be inert). To show they are not isomorphic, consider \[m_\alpha(x)=x^2-x+\frac{1-n}{4}.\] By construction, this has a root in $\mathcal{O}_K$ and therefore has a root in $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ (just reduce your root modulo $2$). On the other hand, since $n \equiv 5 \pmod 8$ we have $m_\alpha(x)=x^2+x+1 \pmod 2$ which by Exercise \ref{ques: irr pol mod 2} we know is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and therefore has no root in $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. So $\mathcal{O}_K/(2)$ is an extension of $\mathbb{F}_2$ by a root of $x^2+x+1$, so its a field, which also goes by the name $\mathbb{F}_4$.

nodes.name: Quadratic reciprocity and splitting
nodes.statement: Using this theorem together with the quadratic reciprocity law, which says \[\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{4}}\] (with $p,q$ primes) we can easily find how primes decompose in quadratic extensions.

nodes.name: Normal extension
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be an extension of number fields. We say $K$ is \textit{normal} over $F$ every embedding $\sigma:K \to \mathbb{C}$ which fixes $F$ has image again in $K$. In other words the embedding $\sigma$ is an automorphism $\sigma:K \to K$ which fixes the elements of $F$. In particular, if $K=F(\alpha)$ and $K$ contains all of the conjugates of $\alpha$, then $K$ is normal.

nodes.name: Q(sqrt2) is normal
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ and $F=\mathbb{Q}$. Then since each embedding that fixes $\mathbb{Q}$ sends $\sqrt{2}$ to one of $\pm \sqrt{2} \in K$, we see that $K$ is normal.

nodes.name: Q(cuberoot 2) is not normal
nodes.statement: If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ then this is not normal, since one of the embeddings will send $\sqrt[3]{2}$ to $\zeta_3\sqrt[3]{2}$ (where $\zeta_3$ is a non-trivial cube root of unity) which is a complex number and therefore not contained in $K$.

nodes.name: Normal closure exists
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields. Then there is a finite extension $L/K$ such that $L/F$ is normal as is $L/K$.
assumptions: Let $K/F$ be a finite extension of number fields.
conclusions: there is a finite extension $L/K$ such that $L/F$ is normal as is $L/K$.
nodes.label: prop: fin ext makes normal

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: If $K=F(\alpha)$, then just set $L=F(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n)$ where $\alpha_i$ are the conjugates of $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Adjoin all conjugates of a primitive element.

nodes.name: Galois action on ideals; Galois group
nodes.statement: If $K/F$ is a normal extension, $\mathfrak{a} \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ is an ideal and $\sigma$ is an embedding of $K$ fixing $F$ (which in particular is an automorphism). Then we let $\sigma(\mathfrak{a})$ be the ideal in $K$ generated by the images of the elements of $\mathfrak{a}$ under $\sigma$. Furthermore, we let $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ denote the set of embeddings of $K$ which fix $F$. Since $K/F$ is normal, this can be made into a group by using composition as our group operation, i.e. $\sigma_1,\sigma_2 \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ we let $(\sigma_1 \sigma_2)(x)= \sigma_1(\sigma_2(x))$. By Proposition \ref{prop: emb extns} there are only $[K:F]$ such embeddings, so this group has size $[K:F]$ and is known as the Galois group.

nodes.name: Galois group acts transitively on primes over p
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a normal extension of number fields. Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$ and $\mathfrak{P},\mathfrak{P}'$ be two prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}_K$ above $\mathfrak{p}$. Then $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal lying over $\mathfrak{p}$, moreover there is some element $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, such that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{P}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Galois conjugates of a prime over $\mathfrak{p}$ are primes over $\mathfrak{p}$, and the Galois group acts transitively on them.
assumptions: Let $K/F$ be a normal extension of number fields. Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_F$ and $\mathfrak{P},\mathfrak{P}'$ be two prime ideals of $\mathcal{O}_K$ above $\mathfrak{p}$.
conclusions: $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal lying over $\mathfrak{p}$, moreover there is some element $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, such that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{P}'$.
nodes.label: thm: ideals and embs

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$. Note that since $\mathfrak{P}$ is a prime ideal $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}$ is a integral domain. Now, apply $\sigma$ to this quotient. Since $\sigma(\mathcal{O}_K)=\mathcal{O}_K$ (as $K/F$ is normal) we get \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P} \cong \mathcal{O}_K /\sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] and therefore $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal. Moreover, since $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$ (this is what lying above means) and $\sigma$ fixes $F$ we see that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P}) \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$. Now, suppose that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P}) 
eq \mathfrak{P}'$ for all $\sigma \in G$. Then we can use the Chinese remainder theorem ef{thm: chinese rem theorem} to find some $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\alpha \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{P}'\] and \[\alpha \equiv 1 \mod \sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] for all $\sigma \in G$. Now, \[N_{K/F}(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}' \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}.\] On the other hand $\alpha 
ot \in \sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ by construction, and therefore $\sigma^{-1}(\alpha) 
ot \in \mathfrak{P}$. But we have \[N_{K/F}(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma^{-1} \in G} \sigma^{-1}(\alpha).\] This gives us a contradiction, since we have just seen that the left hand side is in $\mathfrak{p}$. But the right hand is not contained in $\mathfrak{P}$ since $\sigma^{-1}(\alpha) 
ot \in \mathfrak{P}$, but $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ preserves primality and lying over; transitivity by a CRT element whose norm lies in $\mathfrak{p}$ but avoids $\mathfrak{P}$.

nodes.name: $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ is a prime over $\mathfrak{p}$
nodes.statement: Let $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$. Note that since $\mathfrak{P}$ is a prime ideal $\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}$ is a integral domain. Now, apply $\sigma$ to this quotient. Since $\sigma(\mathcal{O}_K)=\mathcal{O}_K$ (as $K/F$ is normal) we get \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P} \cong \mathcal{O}_K /\sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] and therefore $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal. Moreover, since $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$ (this is what lying above means) and $\sigma$ fixes $F$ we see that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P}) \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}$.

nodes.name: Assume no conjugate equals $\mathfrak{P}'$; choose $\alpha$ by CRT
nodes.statement: Now, suppose that $\sigma(\mathfrak{P}) \neq \mathfrak{P}'$ for all $\sigma \in G$. Then we can use the Chinese remainder theorem \ref{thm: chinese rem theorem} to find some $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\alpha \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{P}'\] and \[\alpha \equiv 1 \mod \sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] for all $\sigma \in G$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume no conjugate equals $\mathfrak{P}'$; choose $\alpha$ by CRT

nodes.name: The norm of $\alpha$ lies in $\mathfrak{p}$ but not in $\mathfrak{P}$:
nodes.statement:
Now, \[N_{K/F}(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}' \cap \mathcal{O}_F=\mathfrak{p}.\] On the other hand $\alpha 
ot \in \sigma(\mathfrak{P})$ by construction, and therefore $\sigma^{-1}(\alpha) 
ot \in \mathfrak{P}$. But we have \[N_{K/F}(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma \in G} \sigma(\alpha)=\prod_{\sigma^{-1} \in G} \sigma^{-1}(\alpha).\] This gives us a contradiction, since we have just seen that the left hand side is in $\mathfrak{p}$. But the right hand is not contained in $\mathfrak{P}$ since $\sigma^{-1}(\alpha) 
ot \in \mathfrak{P}$, but $\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathfrak{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: The norm of $\alpha$ lies in $\mathfrak{p}$ but not in $\mathfrak{P}$: contradiction

nodes.name: Equal e and f in normal extensions
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be a normal extension of number fields and let $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}'$ be two primes lying above the prime $\mathfrak{p}$. Then \[e_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}=e_{\mathfrak{P}'|\mathfrak{p}} \qquad f_{\mathfrak{P}|\mathfrak{p}}=e_{\mathfrak{P}'|\mathfrak{p}}\]
assumptions: Let $K/F$ be a normal extension of number fields and let $\mathfrak{P}$ and $\mathfrak{P}'$ be two primes lying above the prime $\mathfrak{p}$.
nodes.label: cor: ram and inert in gal ext

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Lets start by factoring $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$. We have \[\mathfrak{p} \mathcal{O}_K=\prod_i \mathfrak{P}_i^{e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}}.\] Now, by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals and embs}, if we apply $\sigma$ to this equation we get \[\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K=\sigma(\mathfrak{p})\mathcal{O}_K=\prod_i \sigma(\mathfrak{P}_i)^{e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}}\] but then by the fact that for any $i,j$ we can find $\sigma$ such that $\mathfrak{P}_i=\sigma(\mathfrak{P}_j)$ and uniqueness of factorization, we get that \[e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}=e_{\mathfrak{P}_j|\mathfrak{p}}\] which gives the first part of the result. For the second part, we note that by the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: ideals and embs} we have seen that \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}=:k_{\mathfrak{P}} \cong k_{\sigma(\mathfrak{P})}:=\mathcal{O}_K/\sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] from which the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Galois elements to the factorization of $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$ and use transitivity; residue fields are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Factor $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K$
nodes.statement: Lets start by factoring $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$. We have \[\mathfrak{p} \mathcal{O}_K=\prod_i \mathfrak{P}_i^{e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}}.\]

nodes.name: Transitivity and unique factorization give equal $e$
nodes.statement: Now, by Theorem \ref{thm: ideals and embs}, if we apply $\sigma$ to this equation we get \[\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_K=\sigma(\mathfrak{p})\mathcal{O}_K=\prod_i \sigma(\mathfrak{P}_i)^{e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}}\] but then by the fact that for any $i,j$ we can find $\sigma$ such that $\mathfrak{P}_i=\sigma(\mathfrak{P}_j)$ and uniqueness of factorization, we get that \[e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|\mathfrak{p}}=e_{\mathfrak{P}_j|\mathfrak{p}}\] which gives the first part of the result.
nodes.statement_short: Transitivity and unique factorization give equal $e$

nodes.name: Isomorphic residue fields give equal $f$
nodes.statement: For the second part, we note that by the proof of Theorem \ref{thm: ideals and embs} we have seen that \[\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{P}=:k_{\mathfrak{P}} \cong k_{\sigma(\mathfrak{P})}:=\mathcal{O}_K/\sigma(\mathfrak{P})\] from which the result follows.

nodes.name: Factorization shape in cyclotomic fields
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be an integer and $\zeta_n$ an $n$-th root of unity. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and $p$ a prime number. Then \[(p)=(\mathfrak{p}_1 \mathfrak{p}_2\cdots \mathfrak{p}_r)^e\] where $\mathfrak{p}_i$ are the primes of $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$, which moreover all have the same inertial degree.
assumptions: Let $n$ be an integer and $\zeta_n$ an $n$-th root of unity. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and $p$ a prime number.
conclusions: \[(p)=(\mathfrak{p}_1 \mathfrak{p}_2\cdots \mathfrak{p}_r)^e\] where $\mathfrak{p}_i$ are the primes of $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$, which moreover all have the same inertial degree.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: This follows from Corollary \ref{cor: ram and inert in gal ext} by noting that $K$ is a normal extension.

nodes.name: Ramified primes divide the discriminant
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a prime number and $K$ a number field. If $p$ is ramified in $\mathcal{O}_K$ then $p \mid \Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)$.
assumptions: Let $p$ be a prime number and $K$ a number field.
nodes.label: thm: ram primes div disc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$ such that $e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}>1$. Then we can write $(p)=\mathfrak{p} \mathfrak{a}$ where $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal divisible by all prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$ which are above $p$. Now, let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ be a integral basis for $\mathcal{O}_K$. Since $\mathfrak{a}$ properly contains $(p)$ we can find some $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a}  ackslash (p)$. Then writing \[\alpha=\alpha_1m_1+\dots+\alpha_nm_n\] with $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ we see that since $\alpha 
ot \in (p)$, one of the $m_i$ must not be divisible by $p$. So after relabelling, we can assume $p 
mid m_1$. Now, similar to Proposition ef{prop: disc change of basis} we have that \[\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n)=m_1^2 \Delta(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)=m_1^2\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K).\] Since $p 
mid m_1$ its enough to show that $p \mid \Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n)$. Now, let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ denote the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Let $L$ be a finite extension of $K$ such that $L/\mathbb{Q}$ is normal (which we can do by Proposition ef{prop: fin ext makes normal}). Let $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$. Then the elements of $G$ are just the embeddings of $L$ extending the embeddings of $K$ (if you dont remember what this means go to Definition ef{definition: emb ext}) Since $\alpha$ is contained in $\mathfrak{a}$, its contained in every prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$. It follows that $\alpha$ is also in every prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ in $\mathcal{O}_L$ containing $p$, since each such prime contains $p$ and $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{p}$ is again a prime ideal which contains $p$, hence $\mathfrak{p}$ lies over $p$ and therefore contains $\alpha$. Fix $\mathfrak{P}$ a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$. Then we claim that for any $\sigma \in G$, $\sigma(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}$. To see this note that $\sigma^{-1}(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$ and thus contains $\alpha$. In particular, $\sigma_i(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}$ for all $i$. Therefore, by Proposition ef{prop: disc via embs} $\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n) \in \mathfrak{P}$. But since the discriminant is an integer, we have $\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n) \in \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathbb{Z}=p\mathbb{Z}$ and therefore $p$ divides the discriminant.
nodes.statement_short: Find $\alpha$ in every prime over $p$ replacing a basis vector; all its conjugates lie in a prime $\mathfrak{P}$ of a normal closure, so $p$ divides the discriminant.

nodes.name: Write $(p)=\mathfrak{p}\mathfrak{a}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$ such that $e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}>1$. Then we can write $(p)=\mathfrak{p} \mathfrak{a}$ where $\mathfrak{a}$ is an ideal divisible by all prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_K$ which are above $p$.

nodes.name: Choose $\alpha\in\mathfrak{a}\setminus(p)$ with $p\nmid m_1$
nodes.statement: Now, let $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n$ be a integral basis for $\mathcal{O}_K$. Since $\mathfrak{a}$ properly contains $(p)$ we can find some $\alpha \in \mathfrak{a} \backslash (p)$. Then writing \[\alpha=\alpha_1m_1+\dots+\alpha_nm_n\] with $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ we see that since $\alpha \not \in (p)$, one of the $m_i$ must not be divisible by $p$. So after relabelling, we can assume $p \nmid m_1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $p\mid\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots)$
nodes.statement: Now, similar to Proposition \ref{prop: disc change of basis} we have that \[\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n)=m_1^2 \Delta(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)=m_1^2\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K).\] Since $p \nmid m_1$ its enough to show that $p \mid \Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n)$.

nodes.name: Pass to a normal closure $L$
nodes.statement: Now, let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ denote the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Let $L$ be a finite extension of $K$ such that $L/\mathbb{Q}$ is normal (which we can do by Proposition \ref{prop: fin ext makes normal}). Let $G:=\mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$. Then the elements of $G$ are just the embeddings of $L$ extending the embeddings of $K$ (if you dont remember what this means go to Definition \ref{definition: emb ext})

nodes.name: $\alpha$ lies in every prime of $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$
nodes.statement: Since $\alpha$ is contained in $\mathfrak{a}$, its contained in every prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_K$ over $p$. It follows that $\alpha$ is also in every prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ in $\mathcal{O}_L$ containing $p$, since each such prime contains $p$ and $\mathfrak{P} \cap \mathcal{O}_K=\mathfrak{p}$ is again a prime ideal which contains $p$, hence $\mathfrak{p}$ lies over $p$ and therefore contains $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$ lies in every prime of $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$

nodes.name: Claim: all conjugates of $\alpha$ lie in $\mathfrak{P}$
nodes.statement: Fix $\mathfrak{P}$ a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$. Then we claim that for any $\sigma \in G$, $\sigma(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}$. To see this note that $\sigma^{-1}(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$ and thus contains $\alpha$. In particular, $\sigma_i(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: all conjugates of $\alpha$ lie in $\mathfrak{P}$

nodes.name: Primes over $p$ are permuted by $G$
nodes.statement: To see this note that $\sigma^{-1}(\mathfrak{P})$ is again a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_L$ over $p$ and thus contains $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Hence each $\sigma_i(\alpha)\in\mathfrak{P}$
nodes.statement: In particular, $\sigma_i(\alpha) \in \mathfrak{P}$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Discriminant lies in $\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=p\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: Therefore, by Proposition \ref{prop: disc via embs} $\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n) \in \mathfrak{P}$. But since the discriminant is an integer, we have $\Delta(\alpha,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n) \in \mathfrak{P} \cap \mathbb{Z}=p\mathbb{Z}$ and therefore $p$ divides the discriminant.

nodes.name: Unramified criterion via norm of f'(alpha)
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ for $\alpha$ a primitive element and let $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be any monic polynomial such that $f(\alpha)=0$. If $p$ is a prime number such that $p \nmid N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(f'(\alpha))$ then $p$ is unramified.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field with $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ for $\alpha$ a primitive element and let $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be any monic polynomial such that $f(\alpha)=0$.
nodes.label: cor: p unram if norm of blah

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Since every monic polynomial with $\alpha$ as a root is divisible by $m_\alpha$ (see Proposition \ref{prop: min pol}), its enough to check this for $m_\alpha$. But then Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm} gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $m_\alpha$ and use the discriminant formula.

nodes.name: Finitely many ramified primes
nodes.statement: There are only finitely many primes of\/ $\mathbb{Z}$ which ramify in a number field $K$.

nodes.name: Distinctness of split ideals in quadratic fields
nodes.statement: In (3.4) and (3.6) of Theorem \ref{thm: splitting in quad ext} the ideals appearing are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: The two primes in the split cases of the quadratic splitting theorem are distinct.
nodes.label: cor: ids are disc

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Using Exercise \ref{ques: disc of quad} and Theorem \ref{thm: ram primes div disc} we see that since in each case the prime does not divide the discriminant, the prime cannot be ramified and therefore the ideals are distinct.
nodes.statement_short: The prime does not divide the discriminant, so it is unramified.

nodes.name: Decomposition theorem for cyclotomic fields
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $\zeta_n$ an $n$-th root of unity. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and $p$ a prime number. Write $n=p^km$ with $p \nmid m$ and set $e=\varphi(p^k)$ (where $\varphi$ is Euler's Totient function). Lastly, let $f$ be the (multiplicative) order of $p$ modulo $m$. Then \[(p)=(\mathfrak{p}_1 \mathfrak{p}_2\cdots \mathfrak{p}_r)^e\] (so $e=e_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$) and moreover $f=f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=p^km$, $(p)=(\mathfrak{p}_1\cdots\mathfrak{p}_r)^{\varphi(p^k)}$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ with $f$ the order of $p$ mod $m$.
assumptions: Let $n$ be a positive integer and $\zeta_n$ an $n$-th root of unity. Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ and $p$ a prime number. Write $n=p^km$ with $p \nmid m$ and set $e=\varphi(p^k)$ (where $\varphi$ is Euler's Totient function). Lastly, let $f$ be the (multiplicative) order of $p$ modulo $m$.

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: We start by letting $\alpha=\zeta^m$ and $\beta=\zeta^{p^k}$. So $\alpha$ is a $p^k$-th root of unity and $\beta$ is a $m$-th root of unity. We will prove the theorem by seeing how $(p)$ factorizes in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ and in $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$ and then combining the result. \begin{lemma} With the above notation. In $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ we have \[(p)=(1-\alpha)^{\varphi(p^k)}\] with $(1-\alpha)$ a prime ideal. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} First note that $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(p^k)$ since this is the degree of the $p^k$ cyclotomic polynomial (See Lemma \ref{lem: cyclo poly}). Next, from Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we have $p=u(1-\alpha)^{\varphi(p^k)}$, this tells us that (as ideals in $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$) \[(p)=(1-\alpha)^{\varphi(p^k)}.\] Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} then gives the result. \end{proof} \begin{lemma} In $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$, $p$ is unramified and for each $\mathfrak{p}$ over $p$, we have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Using Corollary \ref{cor: p unram if norm of blah} with $f(x)=x^m-1$, we need to check if $p$ divides \[m^{[\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]}N_{\mathbb{Q}(\beta)/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta^{m-1}).\] But $p \nmid m$ and $\beta$ is a unit, so its norm is $\{\pm 1\}$ therefore $p$ is unramified. So in $\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[(p)=\mathfrak{p}_1\dots\mathfrak{p}_s.\] Moreover, since $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)/\mathbb{Q}$ is normal we know that $f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}=f_{\mathfrak{p}_j|p}$. So let $\mathfrak{p}:=\mathfrak{p}_1$. Its enough to check that $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f$ (where $f$ is as above- the multiplicative order of $p$ modulo $m$). Let $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\mathbb{Z}[\beta]/\mathfrak{p}$. First, recall that $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=[\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}: \mathbb{F}_p]$. So $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=h$ for some $h$. We want to show that $h=f$. We will do this in two steps, by first showing $h \geq f$ and then $h \leq f$. ($h \geq f$): Let $\overline{\beta}$ denote the image of $\beta$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. We will first show that $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. Assume for contradiction this is not the case, then $\overline{\beta}^{m/l} \equiv 1 \pmod \mathfrak{p}$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{p} \mid (\beta^{m/l}-1)$) for some prime factor $l$ of $m$. Now, $\beta^{m/l}$ is an $l$-th root of unity. Then, by Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we see that $\beta^{m/l}-1$ divides $l$ and $l$ is a factor of $m$. Thus $\mathfrak{p} \mid m$. This gives a contradiction as $\mathfrak{p} \mid p$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$. So $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. By Lagrange's theorem this means $m\mid N(\mathfrak{p})-1$ and note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal over $p$, we have $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^h$. Thus $p^h \equiv 1 \pmod m$. But the order of $p$ modulo $m$ is $f$, so we have $h \geq f$. ($h \leq f$): Since $p^f \equiv 1 \pmod m$ it follows that $\beta^{p^f} = \beta$. Now, note that \[(x+y)^{p^f} \equiv x^{p^f}+y^{p^f} \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta].\] This means that for all $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta]\] (also using FLT). Now since $(p) \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we see that \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \pmod \mathfrak{p}.\] Therefore every non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a root of $x^{p^f}-x$. Now, since we are in a field, any polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots. This polynomial has $p^h$ roots (as this is the size of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$) therefore $p^h \leq p^f \implies h \leq f$. This gives the result. \end{proof} Lets now put these two lemmas together and finish proving the theorem. Lemma \ref{lem: lem1} and Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} tells us that \[e_{(1-\alpha)|p} \cdot f_{(1-\alpha)|p}=e \cdot 1=[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(p^k)\] Similarly, Lemma \ref{lem: lem2} gives \[s \cdot e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}\cdot f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=s \cdot 1\cdot f=[\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(m)\] Now, if $\mathfrak{P}_i$ denote the prime ideals of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n]$ over $p$, then we know that \[\sum_i e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|p}f_{\mathfrak{P}_i|p}=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(n)=\varphi(p^k)\varphi(m)\] Lastly, using Proposition \ref{prop: tow law for ram rel} together with \[[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)][\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}(\beta)][\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]\] gives \[s \cdot e \cdot f=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]\] from which the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Split $\zeta_n$ into a $p^k$-th and an $m$-th root of unity; $p$ is totally ramified in the first and unramified with degree $f$ in the second; combine via the fundamental identity.

nodes.name: Set $\alpha=\zeta^m$, $\beta=\zeta^{p^k}$
nodes.statement: We start by letting $\alpha=\zeta^m$ and $\beta=\zeta^{p^k}$. So $\alpha$ is a $p^k$-th root of unity and $\beta$ is a $m$-th root of unity. We will prove the theorem by seeing how $(p)$ factorizes in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ and in $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$ and then combining the result.

nodes.statement: \begin{lemma} With the above notation. Assume for contradiction this is not the case, then $\overline{\beta}^{m/l} \equiv 1 \pmod \mathfrak{p}$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{p} \mid (\beta^{m/l}-1)$) for some prime factor $l$ of $m$. Now, $\beta^{m/l}$ is an $l$-th root of unity. Then, by Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we see that $\beta^{m/l}-1$ divides $l$ and $l$ is a factor of $m$. Thus $\mathfrak{p} \mid m$. This gives a contradiction as $\mathfrak{p} \mid p$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$. So $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. By Lagrange's theorem this means $m\mid N(\mathfrak{p})-1$ and note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal over $p$, we have $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^h$. Thus $p^h \equiv 1 \pmod m$. But the order of $p$ modulo $m$ is $f$, so we have $h \geq f$. ($h \leq f$): Since $p^f \equiv 1 \pmod m$ it follows that $\beta^{p^f} = \beta$. Now, note that \[(x+y)^{p^f} \equiv x^{p^f}+y^{p^f} \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta].\] This means that for all $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta]\] (also using FLT). Now since $(p) \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we see that \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \pmod \mathfrak{p}.\] Therefore every non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a root of $x^{p^f}-x$. Now, since we are in a field, any polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots. This polynomial has $p^h$ roots (as this is the size of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$) therefore $p^h \leq p^f \implies h \leq f$. This gives the result. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Combine the lemmas
nodes.statement: Lets now put these two lemmas together and finish proving the theorem.

nodes.name: $e=\varphi(p^k)$, $f=1$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lem: lem1} and Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} tells us that \[e_{(1-\alpha)|p} \cdot f_{(1-\alpha)|p}=e \cdot 1=[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(p^k)\]

nodes.name: $sf=\varphi(m)$ in $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$
nodes.statement: Similarly, Lemma \ref{lem: lem2} gives \[s \cdot e_{\mathfrak{p}|p}\cdot f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=s \cdot 1\cdot f=[\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(m)\]

nodes.name: Fundamental identity in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$
nodes.statement: Now, if $\mathfrak{P}_i$ denote the prime ideals of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n]$ over $p$, then we know that \[\sum_i e_{\mathfrak{P}_i|p}f_{\mathfrak{P}_i|p}=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=\varphi(n)=\varphi(p^k)\varphi(m)\]

nodes.name: Multiplicativity in towers gives the result
nodes.statement: Lastly, using Proposition \ref{prop: tow law for ram rel} together with \[[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)][\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}]=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}(\beta)][\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]\] gives \[s \cdot e \cdot f=[\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n):\mathbb{Q}]\] from which the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity in towers gives the result

nodes.name: p totally ramified in Q(zeta_{p^k})
nodes.statement: With the above notation. In $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ we have \[(p)=(1-\alpha)^{\varphi(p^k)}\] with $(1-\alpha)$ a prime ideal.
assumptions: With the above notation.
conclusions: In $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ we have \[(p)=(1-\alpha)^{\varphi(p^k)}\] with $(1-\alpha)$ a prime ideal.
nodes.label: lem: lem1

nodes.name: Proof

nodes.name: p unramified with residue degree f in Q(zeta_m)
nodes.statement: In $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$, $p$ is unramified and for each $\mathfrak{p}$ over $p$, we have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f$.
assumptions: In $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$
conclusions: $p$ is unramified and for each $\mathfrak{p}$ over $p$, we have $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f$
nodes.label: lem: lem2

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Using Corollary \ref{cor: p unram if norm of blah} with $f(x)=x^m-1$, we need to check if $p$ divides \[m^{[\mathbb{Q}(\beta):\mathbb{Q}]}N_{\mathbb{Q}(\beta)/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta^{m-1}).\] But $p \nmid m$ and $\beta$ is a unit, so its norm is $\{\pm 1\}$ therefore $p$ is unramified. So in $\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[(p)=\mathfrak{p}_1\dots\mathfrak{p}_s.\] Moreover, since $\mathbb{Q}(\beta)/\mathbb{Q}$ is normal we know that $f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}=f_{\mathfrak{p}_j|p}$. So let $\mathfrak{p}:=\mathfrak{p}_1$. Its enough to check that $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=f$ (where $f$ is as above- the multiplicative order of $p$ modulo $m$). Let $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}:=\mathbb{Z}[\beta]/\mathfrak{p}$. First, recall that $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=[\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}: \mathbb{F}_p]$. So $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=h$ for some $h$. We want to show that $h=f$. We will do this in two steps, by first showing $h \geq f$ and then $h \leq f$. ($h \geq f$): Let $\overline{\beta}$ denote the image of $\beta$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. We will first show that $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. Assume for contradiction this is not the case, then $\overline{\beta}^{m/l} \equiv 1 \pmod \mathfrak{p}$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{p} \mid (\beta^{m/l}-1)$) for some prime factor $l$ of $m$. Now, $\beta^{m/l}$ is an $l$-th root of unity. Then, by Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we see that $\beta^{m/l}-1$ divides $l$ and $l$ is a factor of $m$. Thus $\mathfrak{p} \mid m$. This gives a contradiction as $\mathfrak{p} \mid p$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$. So $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. By Lagrange's theorem this means $m\mid N(\mathfrak{p})-1$ and note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal over $p$, we have $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^h$. Thus $p^h \equiv 1 \pmod m$. But the order of $p$ modulo $m$ is $f$, so we have $h \geq f$. ($h \leq f$): Since $p^f \equiv 1 \pmod m$ it follows that $\beta^{p^f} = \beta$. Now, note that \[(x+y)^{p^f} \equiv x^{p^f}+y^{p^f} \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta].\] This means that for all $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta]\] (also using FLT). Now since $(p) \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we see that \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \pmod \mathfrak{p}.\] Therefore every non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a root of $x^{p^f}-x$. Now, since we are in a field, any polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots. This polynomial has $p^h$ roots (as this is the size of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$) therefore $p^h \leq p^f \implies h \leq f$. This gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Unramified by the norm criterion; residue degree $h=f$ by showing $\bar\beta$ has order $m$ ($h\ge f$) and Frobenius $\gamma^{p^f}=\gamma$ ($h\le f$).

So $f_{\mathfrak{p}|p}=h$ for some $h$. We want to show that $h=f$. We will do this in two steps, by first showing $h \geq f$ and then $h \leq f$.

nodes.name: $h\geq f$
nodes.statement: ($h \geq f$): Let $\overline{\beta}$ denote the image of $\beta$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. We will first show that $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. Assume for contradiction this is not the case, then $\overline{\beta}^{m/l} \equiv 1 \pmod \mathfrak{p}$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{p} \mid (\beta^{m/l}-1)$) for some prime factor $l$ of $m$. Now, $\beta^{m/l}$ is an $l$-th root of unity. Then, by Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we see that $\beta^{m/l}-1$ divides $l$ and $l$ is a factor of $m$. Thus $\mathfrak{p} \mid m$. This gives a contradiction as $\mathfrak{p} \mid p$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$. So $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. By Lagrange's theorem this means $m\mid N(\mathfrak{p})-1$ and note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal over $p$, we have $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^h$. Thus $p^h \equiv 1 \pmod m$. But the order of $p$ modulo $m$ is $f$, so we have $h \geq f$.

nodes.statement: We will first show that $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. Assume for contradiction this is not the case, then $\overline{\beta}^{m/l} \equiv 1 \pmod \mathfrak{p}$ (i.e. $\mathfrak{p} \mid (\beta^{m/l}-1)$) for some prime factor $l$ of $m$. Now, $\beta^{m/l}$ is an $l$-th root of unity. Then, by Exercise \ref{ques: fac of p in p-th root} we see that $\beta^{m/l}-1$ divides $l$ and $l$ is a factor of $m$. Thus $\mathfrak{p} \mid m$. This gives a contradiction as $\mathfrak{p} \mid p$ and $\gcd(m,p)=1$.

nodes.name: Lagrange: $p^h\equiv1 \bmod m$
nodes.statement: So $\overline{\beta}$ has order $m$ in $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$. By Lagrange's theorem this means $m\mid N(\mathfrak{p})-1$ and note that since $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal over $p$, we have $N(\mathfrak{p})=p^h$. Thus $p^h \equiv 1 \pmod m$. But the order of $p$ modulo $m$ is $f$, so we have $h \geq f$.

nodes.name: $h\leq f$
nodes.statement: ($h \leq f$): Since $p^f \equiv 1 \pmod m$ it follows that $\beta^{p^f} = \beta$. Now, note that \[(x+y)^{p^f} \equiv x^{p^f}+y^{p^f} \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta].\] This means that for all $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta]\] (also using FLT). Now since $(p) \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we see that \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \pmod \mathfrak{p}.\] Therefore every non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a root of $x^{p^f}-x$. Now, since we are in a field, any polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots. This polynomial has $p^h$ roots (as this is the size of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$) therefore $p^h \leq p^f \implies h \leq f$. This gives the result.

nodes.name: Frobenius: $\gamma^{p^f}\equiv\gamma$
nodes.statement: Now, note that \[(x+y)^{p^f} \equiv x^{p^f}+y^{p^f} \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta].\] This means that for all $\gamma \in \mathbb{Z}[\beta]$ we have \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \mod p\mathbb{Z}[\beta]\] (also using FLT). Now since $(p) \subset \mathfrak{p}$ we see that \[\gamma^{p^f} \equiv \gamma \pmod \mathfrak{p}.\]

nodes.name: Root count gives $p^h\le p^f$
nodes.statement: Therefore every non-zero element of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$ is a root of $x^{p^f}-x$. Now, since we are in a field, any polynomial of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots. This polynomial has $p^h$ roots (as this is the size of $\mathbb{F}_{\mathfrak{p}}$) therefore $p^h \leq p^f \implies h \leq f$. This gives the result.

nodes.name: Splitting of primes in Q(zeta_5)
nodes.statement: Lets use this theorem to see how primes factorize in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$. \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{ |c | c | c | c |} \hline $p \mod 5$ & Order of $p \mod m$ & Factorization of $(p)$ & Norms \\ \hline $0$ & - & $(p)=\mathfrak{p}^4$ & $N(\mathfrak{p})=p$ \\ \hline $1$ & $1$ & $(p)=\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_4$ & $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p$ \\ \hline $2$ & $4$ & $(p)$ & $N((p))=p^4$ \\ \hline $3$ & $4$ & $(p)$ & $N((p))=p^4$ \\ \hline $4$ & $2$& $(p)=\mathfrak{p}_{1}\mathfrak{p}_2$& $N(\mathfrak{p}_i)=p^2$ \\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center} We can use this to say things about how primes factor in extensions of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_5)$. For example, in $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{55})$ we see that \[(11)=(\mathfrak{p}_1\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_4)^{10}\] with $f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}=1$.

nodes.name: Principal fractional ideals form a subgroup
nodes.statement: Note that furthermore, if $(x)$ and $(y)$ are two principal fractional ideals, then $(x)(y)=(xy)$ is also a fractional ideal and moreover, $(x)(x^{-1})=\mathcal{O}_K$. Thus the set of principal fractional ideals forms a subgroup of $J_K$ (the group of fractional ideal as defined in Proposition \ref{prop: frac ideals form grp}).

nodes.name: Subgroup of principal fractional ideals
nodes.statement: Let $P_K$ denote the subgroup of principal fractional ideals.

nodes.name: Ideal class group and class number
nodes.statement: The \textit{class group} of $K$ is defined to be quotient group \[\mathrm{Cl}_K=\frac{J_K}{P_K}. \] Its elements are called ideal classes. If $\mathfrak{a}$ is a fractional ideal, we let $[\mathfrak{a}]$ denote its class in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$. We let $h_K$ denote the size of $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ (which we will see below is finite), this is called the \textit{class number} of $K$.

nodes.name: Identity and equality in the class group
nodes.statement: Note that in the class group, the identity element is given by the class of principal fractional ideals, which we denote by $[1]$ or $[(1)]$. Furthermore, note that if $\mathfrak{a}$ and $\mathfrak{b}$ are fractional ideals then \[[\mathfrak{a}]=[\mathfrak{b}]\] means that there is some principal fractional ideal $(\alpha)$ such that $\mathfrak{a}=(\alpha)\mathfrak{b}$. So as a SET $[\mathfrak{a}]=\{(x)\mathfrak{a} \mid x \in K\}$.

nodes.name: O_K is a PID iff the class group is trivial
nodes.statement: Note that, $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a PID if and only if $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is trivial.

nodes.name: O_K is a UFD iff the class group is trivial
nodes.statement: Moreover, since a Dedekind domain is a PID if and only if its a UFD, this means that $\mathcal{O}_K$ is a UFD if and only if $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Finiteness of the class group
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field. Then $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is finite.
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field.
nodes.label: thm: cls grp fin

nodes.name: Minkowski bound theorem
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with $r_1$ real embeddings and $r_2$ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings. Let $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=n$ and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$. Then there is an element $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ such that \[|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(a)| \leq \frac{n!}{n^n} \left( \frac{4}{\pi} \right)^{r_2} |\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)|^{1/2} N(\mathfrak{a}) \]
nodes.statement_short: Every ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ contains a nonzero $a$ with $|N(a)|\le M_K N(\mathfrak{a})$.
also_stated_at: Let $K$ be a number field with $r_1$ real embeddings and $r_2$ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings. Let $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=n$ and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$. Then there is an element $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ such that \[|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(a)| \leq \frac{n!}{n^n} \left( \frac{4}{\pi} \right)^{r_2} |\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)|^{1/2} N(\mathfrak{a}) \]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field with $r_1$ real embeddings and $r_2$ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings. Let $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=n$ and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_K$.
conclusions: there is an element $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ such that \[|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(a)| \leq \frac{n!}{n^n} \left( \frac{4}{\pi} \right)^{r_2} |\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)|^{1/2} N(\mathfrak{a}) \]
nodes.label: thm: mink bound

nodes.name: Minkowski bound
nodes.statement: The quantity $ \frac{n!}{n^n} \left( \frac{4}{\pi} \right)^{r_2} |\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)|^{1/2}$ is known as the Minkowski bound and we will denote it by $M_K$.

nodes.name: Each ideal class has a representative of norm at most M_K
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and let $C$ be an ideal class in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$. Then $C$ contains an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[N(\mathfrak{a}) \leq M_K.\]
assumptions: Let $K$ be a number field and let $C$ be an ideal class in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$.
conclusions: $C$ contains an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[N(\mathfrak{a}) \leq M_K.\]
nodes.label: prop: each ideal class has rep of small norm

nodes.name: Proof
nodes.statement: Consider the class $C^{-1}$. This has a representative which is an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$. By Theorem \ref{thm: mink bound} there is an $x \in \mathfrak{b}$ such that $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x)| \leq M_K N(\mathfrak{b})$. Set $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}^{-1} (x)$. Then this is in the same class as $C$ since its a multiple of $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ by a principal ideal $(x)$. Moreover, since $x \in \mathfrak{b}$ it follows that $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}(x) \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ (recall that $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}=\{y \in K | y\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K\}$ ), so $\mathfrak{a}$ is a proper ideal. Now by construction \[N(\mathfrak{a})=\frac{|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x)|}{N(\mathfrak{b})} \leq M_K\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Minkowski bound to an ideal in $C^{-1}$ and take $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}^{-1}(x)$.

nodes.name: Small element $x$ in an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ of $C^{-1}$
nodes.statement: Consider the class $C^{-1}$. This has a representative which is an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$. By Theorem \ref{thm: mink bound} there is an $x \in \mathfrak{b}$ such that $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x)| \leq M_K N(\mathfrak{b})$.
nodes.statement_short: Small element $x$ in an ideal $\mathfrak{b}$ of $C^{-1}$

nodes.name: $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}^{-1}(x)$ is an integral ideal in $C$
nodes.statement: Set $\mathfrak{a}=\mathfrak{b}^{-1} (x)$. Then this is in the same class as $C$ since its a multiple of $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}$ by a principal ideal $(x)$. Moreover, since $x \in \mathfrak{b}$ it follows that $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}(x) \subset \mathcal{O}_K$ (recall that $\mathfrak{b}^{-1}=\{y \in K | y\mathfrak{b} \subset \mathcal{O}_K\}$ ), so $\mathfrak{a}$ is a proper ideal.

nodes.name: Norm bound
nodes.statement: Now by construction \[N(\mathfrak{a})=\frac{|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x)|}{N(\mathfrak{b})} \leq M_K\] which gives the result.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{thm: cls grp fin}
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: each ideal class has rep of small norm} each ideal class $C$ in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ must contain an ideal of norm at most $M_K$. Now Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm} implies there are only finitely many such ideals. So there are only finitely many ideal classes.
nodes.statement_short: Each class has a representative of bounded norm and there are finitely many ideals of each norm.

nodes.name: Representatives of norm at most $M_K$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{prop: each ideal class has rep of small norm} each ideal class $C$ in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ must contain an ideal of norm at most $M_K$.

nodes.name: Finitely many such ideals
nodes.statement: Now Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm} implies there are only finitely many such ideals. So there are only finitely many ideal classes.

nodes.name: Class group of Q(i) is trivial
nodes.statement: Let $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Lets look at $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$. Using Proposition \ref{prop: num field disc in terms of norm} we see that $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)=-4$. Moreover, $K$ has no real embeddings, so $r_1=0$ and $r_2=1$. Putting this together we get \[M_K=\frac{2!}{2^2} \left(\frac{4}{\pi}\right)\sqrt{4}=\frac{4}{\pi} \approxeq 1.273.\] Theorem \ref{thm: mink bound} tells us that each ideal class contains an ideal of norm $\leq 1$. But the only ideal of norm $1$ is the trivial ideal. So $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is trivial. If follows that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a PID.

nodes.name: Class number one imaginary quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Show that if $d \in \{-1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163\}$ then $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$ has trivial class group and is thus a PID.

nodes.name: Class group of Q(sqrt-5) has order 2
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$. From Theorem \ref{thm: int quad field} we know that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$. Here again we have $r_1=0$, $r_2=1$ and $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)=-20$. Therefore \[M_K=\frac{2!}{2^2} \left(\frac{4}{\pi}\right)\sqrt{20}=\sqrt{80 \pi}< 3\] This means every class contains an ideal of norm $1$ or $2$. We know the trivial ideal has norm $1$, so lets look at what ideal has norm $2$. As we saw in the proof of Corollary \ref{cor: fin many ideals of given norm}, its enough to look at what prime ideals divide $2$. By Theorem \ref{thm: splitting in quad ext} we have \[(2)=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})^2\] and therefore $\mathfrak{p}_2:=(2,1+\sqrt{-5})$ is the unique ideal of norm $2$. So, this means the class group $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ has either $1$ or $2$ elements, depending of whether or not these two ideals are in the same class, i.e., if $[1]=[\mathfrak{p}_2]$. In other words, is $\mathfrak{p}_2$ a principal ideal (since principal ideals are the things which $[1]$ consists of). If it where principal, then Proposition \ref{prop: ideal norm coincides with other norm} would mean that there is some element in $\mathcal{O}_K$ of norm $\pm 2$. Now \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x+y\sqrt{-5})=x^2+5y^2\] and its easy to see that this is never equal to $\pm 2$. So $\mathfrak{p}_2$ is not principal and therefore \[\mathrm{Cl}_K=\{[1],[\mathfrak{p}_2]\}\] so $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is cyclic of order $2$.
nodes.label: exmp: class group -5

nodes.name: Class group of Q(cuberoot 7) is cyclic of order 3
nodes.statement: Lets look at $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{7})$ and let $\alpha=\sqrt[3]{7}$. The minimal polynomial is clearly $x^3-7$ which has discriminant $-1323=-3^3 \cdot7^2$. Next, lets check that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt[3]{7}]$. For this we need to check if any of \[\frac{x_2\alpha^2+x_1\alpha+x_0}{3} \qquad \text{ or } \qquad \frac{y_2\alpha^2+y_1\alpha+y_0}{7}\] can be algebraic integers for $0 \leq x_i \leq 2$, $0\leq y_i \leq 6$. Since the minimal polynomial is clearly Eisenstein at $7$ we know from Lemma \ref{lem: eis crit and alg ints} that we only need to worry about $3$. Here is a trick: note that \[(x+7)^3-7\] is Eisenstein at $3$ and at $7$ so if $\beta$ is one of its roots, then $\mathbb{Z}[\beta]=\mathcal{O}_{K'}$ where $K'=\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$, but $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)=\mathbb{Q}(\beta)$ and $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]=\mathbb{Z}[\beta]$. Therefore $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt[3]{7}]$. Knowing this means we can freely use Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum}. Now, lets calculate the Minkowski bound. In this case $n=3$, $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)=-1323$, and $r_1=r_2=1$. Putting this together we get \[M_K=\frac{3!}{3^3}\left(\frac{4}{\pi}\right) \sqrt{1323}= \frac{56\sqrt{3}}{3\pi} \approxeq 10.3\] So we need to find all ideals of norm at most $10$. So lets factor the ideals given by $2,3,5,7$ using Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum}. \begin{itemize} \item $x^3-7 \equiv (x-1)(x^2+x+1) \mod 2$ \item $x^3-7 \equiv (x-1)^3 \mod 3$ \item $x^3-7 \equiv (x-3)(x^2+3x-1) \mod 5$ \item $x^3-7 \equiv x^3 \mod 7$ \end{itemize} From this we deduce \begin{itemize} \item $(2)=\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_2'=(2,\alpha-1)(2,\alpha^2+\alpha+1)$ \item $(3)=\mathfrak{p}_3^3=(3,\alpha-1)^3$ \item $(5)=\mathfrak{p}_5\mathfrak{p}_5'=(5,\alpha-3)(5,\alpha^2+3\alpha-1)$ \item $(7)=\mathfrak{p}_7^3=(7,\alpha)^3=(\alpha)^3$ \end{itemize} By Theorem \ref{thm: ram-rel} we know that $N({\mathfrak{p}_i})=p^{f_{\mathfrak{p}_i|p}}$ so if we calculate the residue degrees, we will know the norms of these ideals. But again Theorem \ref{thm: ded-kum} tells us that this is exactly the degrees of the polynomials appearing on the right hand side of each factorization modulo $p$. So combining this we have: \begin{itemize} \item $N(\mathfrak{p}_2)=2$ and $N(\mathfrak{p}_2')=4$ \item $N(\mathfrak{p}_3)=3$ \item $N(\mathfrak{p}_5)=5$ and $N(\mathfrak{p}_5')=25$ \item $N(\mathfrak{p}_7)=7$ \end{itemize} So by combining these ideals we can construct any ideal of norm at most $10$. The next question is are these ideals distinct in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$? Lets see if any of them are principal: Clearly, $(7)=(\alpha)^3$ is principal so this gives the trivial class in the class group. Note that since $(2)=\mathfrak{p}_2\mathfrak{p}_2'$ we have $[\mathfrak{p}_2]^{-1}=[\mathfrak{p}_2']$. So lets look at the other ideals. Note that \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x+y\alpha+z\alpha^2)=x^3+7y^3+49z^3-21xyz.\] So, do we have elements of norm $2,3$ or $5$? We'll from the above we see that the norm of an element must be a cube modulo $7$. But the only cubes modulo $7$ are $\pm 1$. So there are no elements of norm $2,3,5$. So these ideals are not principal. So $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is generated by $\mathfrak{p}_{2},\mathfrak{p}_3,\mathfrak{p}_5$. The next question is, do these ideals give distinct classes in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$? First note that $\mathfrak{p}_3^3=(3)$ therefore $[\mathfrak{p}_3]$ has order $3$ in $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ (since we already know its not trivial). Note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(2+\sqrt[3]{7})=15$ and $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(-1+\sqrt[3]{7})=6$. Therefore, since we only have one prime ideal of norm $2,3$ and $5$ we must have \[(2+\sqrt[3]{7})=\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_5 \qquad (-1+\sqrt[3]{7})=\mathfrak{p}_3\mathfrak{p}_2 \] thus $[\mathfrak{p}_5][\mathfrak{p}_3]=[1]$ and $[\mathfrak{p}_{2}][\mathfrak{p}_3]=[1]$ giving $[\mathfrak{p}_5]=[\mathfrak{p}_3]^{-1}=[\mathfrak{p}_2]$. Thus $\mathrm{Cl}_K$ is generated by $[\mathfrak{p}_3]$ and is therefore cyclic of order $3$. The multiplication table is then \begin{center} \begin{tabular} {|c| c c c |} \hline &$[1]$&[$\mathfrak{p}_3]$&[$\mathfrak{p}_3^2$]\\ \hline $[1]$&$[1]$&$[\mathfrak{p}_3]$&$[\mathfrak{p}_3^2]$\\ $[\mathfrak{p}_3]$&$[\mathfrak{p}_3] $& $[\mathfrak{p}_3^2]$&$[1]$\\ $[\mathfrak{p}_3^2]$&$[\mathfrak{p}_3^2]$&$[1]$&$[\mathfrak{p}_3]$\\ \hline \end{tabular} \end{center}

nodes.name: Computing the class group
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Find the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ and the discriminant $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)$ (as defined in Definition \ref{definition: disc of num field} ). As we have seen in the problem sheet, in many cases (but not all) we can calculate the discriminant using Theorem \ref{thm: disc of trinom}. \item Find how many real $r_1$ and complex conjugate $r_2$ embeddings our number field $K$ has. To do this, you need to write down the embeddings (all $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ of them) and see how many of them are real or complex. How do you do this quickly? If $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ then look at the conjugates of $\alpha$. With this $r_1$ will be the number of conjugates of $\alpha$ that are real numbers and $r_2$ will be half the number conjugates that are complex. \item Compute the Minkowski bound \[M_K= \frac{n!}{n^n} \left( \frac{4}{\pi} \right)^{r_2} |\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)|^{1/2}\] where $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$. \item Find all ideals of norm $\leq \lfloor M_K \rfloor$. To do this, look at all the primes $p$ less than $\lfloor M_K \rfloor$ and factor the ideal $(p)$ in $\mathcal{O}_K$ using Corollary \ref{cor: ded-kum for K/Q}, or if we are in a quadratic field, use Theorem \ref{thm: splitting in quad ext} which makes things really quick. \item After doing this you will have a list of prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_i$ all with norm $\leq \lfloor M_K \rfloor$. The next step is to see if any of them are trivial in the class group. This means, we need to check if $[\mathfrak{p}_i]=[1]$, in other words is $\mathfrak{p}_i$ principal?\footnote{Warning: Just because Corollary \ref{cor: ded-kum for K/Q} says $\mathfrak{p}_i=(p,something)$ doesn't mean this ideal can't be principal.} How does one do this? Well if $\mathfrak{p}_i$ was principal, it would be generated by an element $\beta$ such that $|N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\beta)|=N((\beta))=N(\mathfrak{p}_i)$. Now check if this gives a contradiction by looking at the possibilities for the norm of $\beta$. \item After this we now have a possibly smaller list of prime ideals, all of which we know are not principal. The next question is to check if they are distinct from one another. In other words, if $[\mathfrak{p}]=[\mathfrak{q}]$. In general this might be difficult, but in the examples above, we have seen some tricks how to do this. \item Once this is all done, we have our final set of generators, and by this point we know the size of the group and it should be easy to write down the multiplication table for the class group. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\mathcal{O}_K$, $\Delta$, signature and Minkowski bound; factor small primes; test principality via norms and identify relations.

nodes.name: Find $\mathcal{O}_K$ and $\Delta(\mathcal{O}_K)$

As we have seen in the problem sheet, in many cases (but not all) we can calculate the discriminant using Theorem \ref{thm: disc of trinom}.
